title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
About this lecture
Mendel’s laws predict ratios, such as 3:1 or 9:3:3:1. Real crosses give counts, such as 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. Today we connect the two.

Probability rules: the product rule (AND), the sum rule (OR) and conditional probability (“given that …”).
Families: the chance that 2 of 4 children are affected (the binomial), and “at least one”.
Testing a ratio: why observed counts never match the expected ones exactly, and the χ² goodness-of-fit test, which tells us whether the gap is bigger than chance would give.
p-values: what they mean, what “fail to reject” means, and Fisher’s claim that Mendel’s data fit too well.

Book: Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter (the sections on probability and on the chi-square test).

Set the scene: last lecture gave the laws of segregation and independent assortment and the ratios they predict. Today is about the bridge between a predicted ratio and a real pile of seeds or children. Two halves. First, probability rules, which they met at upper-secondary school: we recap them with genetics examples and add two new tools, conditional probability and the binomial. Second, the chi-square test, which most of them have only heard of by name. We build it from scratch, with Mendel’s own numbers. Reassure them that the maths stays at fractions and squaring. The one formula to take away is the sum of (O minus E) squared over E.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: A cross is a random experiment
text:
A cross is a random experiment
Each child (or seed) of Aa × Aa is a fresh, independent draw:

each parent passes on A or a with probability ½ each (segregation);
the egg and the sperm are chosen independently of each other;
one child’s genotype says nothing about the next child’s genotype.

So a Punnett square is a probability table: each cell is one equally likely outcome. “3:1” means P(dominant phenotype) = ¾ for each offspring. It is not a promise that exactly 3 out of every 4 will be dominant.
Two rules let us combine these probabilities, and we use them all through the course: in pedigrees, in mapping and in population genetics.

Recap from upper-secondary school and from the Mendel lecture. The key reframe is that a ratio is a probability per offspring, not a quota for a family. Students often believe that if the first three children are unaffected the fourth “must” be affected. Kill this now: each child is an independent draw, and the coin has no memory. Mention that this simple model assumes complete dominance, no lethality and fair segregation. The Extensions to Mendel unit relaxes these assumptions.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Product rule and sum rule


Product rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), if A and B are independent.
Sum rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), if A and B are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen).


Walk through the square. Each cell is “this egg AND this sperm”: the two gametes are independent, so we multiply, half times half is a quarter. The dominant phenotype is “AA OR Aa OR aA”: these cells are mutually exclusive (a child has one genotype), so we add, giving three quarters. Point out the two conditions: multiply only for independent events, add only for events that cannot happen together. A common error is to add probabilities of events that overlap. Note also that all cells sum to 1, which is a free check on any calculation.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Using both rules: a dihybrid cross
text:
Using both rules: a dihybrid cross
AaBb × AaBb, with the two genes on different chromosomes (independent assortment):

P(aabb) = P(aa) × P(bb) = ¼ × ¼ = 1/16
P(A_B_) = P(A_) × P(B_) = ¾ × ¾ = 9/16
P(A_bb or aaB_) = 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16

This works for any number of genes. For AaBbCc × AaBbCc:
P(aabbcc) = \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{64}
No 64-cell Punnett square is needed. Split the cross into one gene at a time, then multiply.

This is the payoff of the product rule: the forked-line or “one gene at a time” method. Independent assortment is exactly the statement that the genes are independent events, so their probabilities multiply. Do the trihybrid on the board to show how much faster it is than a Punnett square. Warn: this only holds for unlinked genes. Linked genes break independence, and that is the Linkage unit. The 9/16 and 1/16 are the 9 and 1 of 9:3:3:1, which we test with chi-square later today.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Conditional probability: “given that …”
Two Aa carriers have a child who is unaffected. What is the chance that this child is a carrier?

Knowing something shrinks the table. We only count the outcomes that are still possible:
P(\text{carrier} \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{P(\text{carrier and unaffected})}{P(\text{unaffected})} = \frac{1/2}{3/4} = \frac23

This is the single most-used calculation in pedigree risk, and the classic exam trap: students answer one half, which is the carrier probability before we knew the phenotype. Once we know the child is unaffected, the aa cell is impossible, so we renormalise over the three remaining equally likely cells, two of which are carriers. Read the vertical bar as “given”. The formula is just the picture written down: the share of the remaining area that is carrier. Preview: in the Pedigrees unit we chain this, for example the probability that two unaffected siblings of affected children have an affected child is 2/3 times 2/3 times 1/4.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Families: how many children are affected?
text:
Families: how many children are affected?
Aa × Aa, four children. Each child is affected (aa) with p = ¼. What is P(exactly 2 affected)?

P(k \text{ of } n) = \binom{n}{k}\, p^k\, (1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} \text{ ("$n$ choose $k$")}

Build the binomial from the two rules. One particular birth order, such as affected, affected, unaffected, unaffected, has probability a quarter times a quarter times three quarters times three quarters by the product rule. There are 6 such orders, which are mutually exclusive, so by the sum rule we multiply by 6. The 6 is “4 choose 2”: the number of ways to pick which 2 of the 4 children are the affected ones. Count them on the slide. Only then show the general formula, and say that n choose k is just that count. For small n they can list the orders by hand. Point out the bar chart: the most likely family has 1 affected child, not “exactly one quarter of 4”. Bars sum to 1.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
“At least one”: use the complement
P(at least one of 4 children affected) has many cases (1, 2, 3 or 4). The opposite event has only one case:
P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac34\right)^4 = 1 - \tfrac{81}{256} \approx 0.68

“None affected” means every child is unaffected, so by the product rule it is (¾)⁴.
Not 4 × ¼ = 1, which would make an affected child certain. Adding is wrong here, because “child 1 affected” and “child 2 affected” can both happen.


The complement trick is a standard move. The wrong answer, 4 times a quarter equals 1, is worth showing because many students produce it: it adds events that are not mutually exclusive, which breaks the sum rule’s condition. With 5 children the naive sum would exceed 1, which is an obvious absurdity. Check against the bar chart on the previous slide: 1 minus 0.316 is 0.684.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Real counts deviate from the ratio
text:
Real counts deviate from the ratio

Every dot is a family simulated with the 3:1 rule exactly true. With 20 seeds the fraction ranges from 0.50 to 0.90. With 2000 seeds it stays close to 0.75.

Deviation from the expected ratio is normal. It is sampling variation, or chance.
Small samples deviate a lot (in proportion); large samples deviate little.
The question is never “does it match exactly?” but “is the deviation larger than chance would usually produce?”


This is the motivation for a statistical test. Everything here obeys 3:1 perfectly, and yet a family of 20 can come out 10 to 10, which looks like 1:1. So we cannot judge by eye. We need a yardstick for how big a deviation chance produces, and that yardstick depends on sample size. The chi-square test is that yardstick. Note the data were simulated in R with rbinom and a fixed seed; students simulate the same thing in the exercise.

The χ² statistic
Turn “how far is observed (O) from expected (E)?” into one number:
\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{classes}} \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}

Square, so that positive and negative deviations do not cancel.
Divide by E, so that a deviation of 19 counts for more when only 1831 were expected than when 5493 were.


Do this slowly on the board. Expected counts come from the total times the hypothesised proportion, never from the ratio numbers themselves. The deviations always sum to zero, which is a useful check. Why square: otherwise plus and minus cancel. Why divide by E: a deviation of 19 is small relative to 5493 and relatively larger relative to 1831. Under the null hypothesis the counts vary by roughly the square root of E, so dividing the squared deviation by E puts every class on the same scale. A chi-square of 0 is a perfect fit; bigger means a worse fit. Now we need to know what values chance alone produces.

Degrees of freedom
The degrees of freedom (df) count how many classes are free to vary once the total is fixed.

2 classes (round, wrinkled): once N and the round count are known, the wrinkled count is fixed. df = 1.
k classes, with the ratio given in advance: df = k − 1.

More classes give more terms in the sum, so χ² tends to be bigger by chance alone. The df tells us which reference curve to use.

Keep df concrete: it is the number of independent counts. With k classes and a fixed total, k minus 1 of them determine the last. That is the rule for a goodness-of-fit test against a ratio given in advance, which is every test today. Mention briefly that if you estimate a parameter from the data, as in the Hardy-Weinberg test, you lose another degree of freedom; that comes in the Hardy-Weinberg unit. The average value of chi-square under the null hypothesis is equal to df, which is a nice anchor: chi-square of 0.26 on 1 df is below average.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
The χ² distribution

If H0 is true, repeating the experiment many times gives χ² values that follow this curve. Most are small; large values are rare.

The curve is what chance alone produces when the hypothesis is true and the counts are large enough. The df = 1 curve is piled up near zero; with more df the bulk moves right, and its average equals df. The dashed lines cut off the top 5% of each curve. A chi-square beyond that line would happen less than 1 time in 20 if H0 were true. In the exercise they simulate 10 000 F2 samples under 3:1 and see their histogram trace exactly the df = 1 curve. That is the honest meaning of this curve.

Rule: if χ² > the 5% critical value (p < 0.05), reject H0: the deviation is too big to blame on chance.
Mendel’s seeds: χ² = 0.263 < 3.84, so p > 0.05 (exactly, p = 0.61). The data are consistent with 3:1.


Define the p-value in words before showing any number: assuming the hypothesis is true, how often would chance give a fit this bad or worse? A small p-value means “rarely”, so we doubt the hypothesis. The table is how this was done before computers, and it is still how they will do it in an exam: compare the statistic with the critical value for the right df. Read the table: going right gives stricter thresholds; going down, more df need a bigger chi-square. For Mendel’s seeds, a p of 0.61 means that 61% of honest 3:1 experiments with 7324 seeds would deviate at least this much. Stress that 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
“Fail to reject” is not “proven”

p < 0.05: the data are unlikely under H0. We reject H0. (We may still be wrong in 1 in 20 tests of a true H0.)
p ≥ 0.05: we fail to reject H0. The data are consistent with H0, but this does not prove it.

Other ratios may fit too: 5474:1850 is also consistent with 2.95:1.
Small samples can rarely reject anything. 6:4 seeds gives χ² = 1.2 against 3:1 (p = 0.27).

A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true.


This is the conceptual heart of the second half. Hypothesis tests are asymmetric: they can give evidence against a hypothesis, but a non-significant result is an absence of evidence, not proof. Use the 6:4 example: with 10 seeds even a ratio that looks like 1.5:1 cannot be told apart from 3:1. Mention the two errors in plain words: rejecting a true hypothesis (which happens 5% of the time by design) and failing to reject a false one (common in small samples). The last bullet is the most common misreading of p-values in published papers too.

Two practical rules, both frequent exam and lab-report errors. Percentages: chi-square scales with N, because the same proportional deviation is far more convincing with more data. Feeding percentages in silently pretends N is 100. Expected counts of at least 5: the smooth chi-square curve is an approximation to a discrete reality. title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Fisher: Mendel’s data fit too well
text:
Fisher: Mendel’s data fit too well


In 1936 R. A. Fisher added up χ² over many of Mendel’s experiments. The total was smaller than chance would usually allow.
With honest sampling, p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1. A whole series of p-values close to 1 is itself suspicious.
Here: the 7 monohybrid experiments give a total of 2.14 on 7 df. A fit this close happens only about 1 time in 20.

Possible explanations include unconscious bias in classifying ambiguous seeds, selective reporting, or an assistant “helping”. The debate continues; you will look up a modern analysis in the exercise.

A lovely twist that shows the test cutting both ways. Under a true hypothesis, chi-square should average about df. Mendel’s seven experiments sum to 2.14 when we expect about 7. Fisher’s full analysis over all of Mendel’s experiments gave an even more extreme left-tail probability. Present this fairly: nobody doubts Mendel’s laws, which have been confirmed countless times; the question is how the published numbers came about. Explanations range from honest misclassification of borderline phenotypes, to stopping counting when the ratio looked right, to deliberate tidying. In the exercise students find a modern reanalysis in PubMed and estimate the left-tail probability by simulation in R.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Where this leads

Extensions to Mendel: modified ratios such as 9:7 and 12:3:1. You use χ² to decide which ratio fits.
Pedigrees: conditional probability and the product rule give carrier and disease risks in families.
Linkage: a χ² test against 1:1:1:1 is the first test for whether two genes are linked.
Hardy–Weinberg: χ² again, with one df lost because the allele frequency is estimated from the data.
In R (this unit’s exercise): chisq.test, pchisq, dbinom, and simulation with replicate().


Chi-square is the workhorse statistic of transmission genetics, and it returns in nearly every unit of Part 1 and Part 2. Point out the new R idiom, simulation under the null hypothesis with replicate, because it is a general way to get a p-value for any statistic, even when no textbook curve exists. That idea comes back in drift simulations and in the Hardy-Weinberg unit.

title: Quiz: pedigree analysis
text:
Short questions on reading pedigrees and on simple risk calculations. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless a question says otherwise, assume one gene, full penetrance and no new mutations.

Q1. Why do human geneticists use pedigrees, when geneticists studying peas or flies use controlled crosses?






Hint





Think about who chooses the parents, how many children there are, and how long a generation takes.









Answer





We cannot set up crosses in humans: people choose their own partners, families have only a few children, and a generation takes 25–30 years. So we collect the crosses that have already happened: who is affected and how they are related. With so few children, ratios such as 3:1 are hardly visible within one family. Instead we look for transmissions that are impossible under a mode.




Q2. Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which modes of inheritance does this rule out: AR, AD, XR, XD?






Hint





Take each mode in turn. Under that mode, what genotype must the daughter have, and could two unaffected parents give it to her?









Answer






AD is ruled out: an affected child needs at least one affected parent.
XD is ruled out: the daughter needs an XA from one parent, and both are unaffected.
XR is ruled out: an affected daughter is XaXa, so she got Xa from her father, who would then be affected.
AR remains: both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa).

One trio with an affected daughter of unaffected parents leaves only autosomal recessive.




Q3. An affected man has an affected son. The son’s mother is unaffected. Which mode does this rule out, and why? Does it rule out X-linked recessive?






Hint





Which chromosome does a father give to his son?









Answer





A father gives his son a Y, not his X. So the son cannot have got an X-linked allele from his father.

XD is ruled out: the son needs XA from his mother, and she is unaffected, so she has none.
XR is not strictly ruled out: the son could have got Xa from a carrier mother, who is unaffected. But this needs a carrier to marry into the family, which is unlikely for a rare allele. So male-to-male transmission makes XR very unlikely.

Male-to-male transmission is the classic evidence for autosomal inheritance.




Q4. An affected woman with an X-linked recessive disease has children with an unaffected man. What do you expect among their sons and their daughters?






Hint





Write her genotype with Xa and XA, then make a Punnett square with his XA and Y.









Answer





She is XaXa and he is XAY.

All sons get Xa from her and Y from him: XaY, all affected.
All daughters get Xa from her and XA from him: XAXa, unaffected carriers.

So an affected woman with even one unaffected son rules out XR.




Q5. Look at the autosomal recessive pedigree in the lecture (fig02). Why are III-2 and III-3 called obligate carriers, even though nobody has tested them?











Hint





What genotype must IV-1 have, and where did each of her two alleles come from?









Answer





IV-1 and IV-3 are affected, so they are aa. Each got one a from each parent. Both parents are unaffected, so each must be Aa. The logic of the pedigree forces it: no test is needed. “Obligate” means must be.




Q6. Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive). What is the probability that their unaffected son is a carrier? Why is it not 1/2?






Hint





Start from Aa × Aa. Which part of the outcomes can you cross out, given that he is unaffected?









Answer





Aa × Aa gives ¼ AA, ½ Aa, ¼ aa. He is unaffected, so he is not aa. Conditional on that:
\[P(Aa \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{1/2}{1/4 + 1/2} = \frac{2}{3}.\]
It is not 1/2 because the 1/2 is a share of all children, including the affected ones. Once we know he is unaffected, the aa quarter is gone, and two of the three remaining quarters are Aa.




Q7. The son from Q6 has a child with a woman from a population with a carrier frequency of 1/25. She has no family history. What is the risk that their child has cystic fibrosis?






Hint





Three things must all happen. Multiply their probabilities (product rule).









Answer





\[P = \underbrace{\tfrac23}_{\text{he is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac1{25}}_{\text{she is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac14}_{\text{both pass }a} = \frac{2}{300} = \frac{1}{150} \approx 0.0067.\]




Q8. An affected man with an X-linked dominant disease has four children with an unaffected woman. Predict the phenotypes of his sons and daughters. Under autosomal dominant inheritance, what is the probability of exactly the same outcome?






Hint





Under XD, what does a father give to each daughter and to each son? Under AD, each child is an independent coin toss.









Answer





Under XD he gives his XA to every daughter and his Y to every son: all daughters affected, all sons unaffected.
Under AD (Aa × aa) each child is affected with probability ½, independently of sex. The chance that the four children show exactly the XD pattern (every daughter affected, every son unaffected) is (½)4 = 1/16. One such family is suggestive; several such families make XD much more likely than AD.




Q9. Why does consanguinity (for example, a first-cousin marriage) increase the risk of recessive disease, but not of dominant disease?






Hint





For a recessive disease, both parents must carry the same rare allele. How likely is that for unrelated partners, and for cousins?









Answer





Relatives share alleles inherited from common ancestors. If a grandparent carried a rare recessive allele, it can reach both cousins and meet again in their child: the child of first cousins is homozygous by descent at about 1/16 of its genes. For unrelated partners, both carrying the same rare allele is very unlikely. A dominant disease needs only one copy, so it shows in the carrier parent anyway; the parents being related adds no new risk.




Q10. An autosomal dominant disease shows up in generations I and III of a family, but the person in generation II who links them is unaffected. Give two explanations.






Hint





One explanation is about the link between genotype and phenotype; the other is about where the allele came from.









Answer






Incomplete penetrance: the person in generation II carries the dominant allele but does not show the disease. They are an obligate carrier.
New mutation in generation III, so the allele in III was not inherited through generation II. (It is also possible that the disease in generation I has a different cause, or that biological parentage differs from the drawn pedigree.)

These are the cases where the strict rule “every affected person has an affected parent” breaks down.




Q11. A clinic collects families with three children, in which both parents are carriers of a recessive disease. It finds them through an affected child. Is the fraction of affected children among these families 1/4? If not, is it higher or lower, and why?






Hint





Which Aa × Aa families never come to the clinic?









Answer





It is higher, about 0.43 rather than 0.25. Aa × Aa families with three unaffected children (probability (3/4)3 ≈ 0.42) never come to the clinic, so they are missing from the count. Among the families that are seen, the expected number of affected children is
\[\frac{nq}{1 - (1-q)^n} = \frac{3 \times 1/4}{1 - (3/4)^3} \approx 1.30,\]
that is 1.30/3 ≈ 0.43 per child. This is ascertainment bias: how families are found changes the ratio we observe.

Risk formulas.

Unaffected child of Aa × Aa: \(P(Aa \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{1/2}{3/4} = \frac{2}{3}\).
Child affected (AR) = P(mother is Aa) × P(father is Aa) × ¼.
Ascertainment: in sibships of size n where each child is affected with probability q, families with at least one affected child have on average \(\dfrac{nq}{1-(1-q)^n}\) affected children.

text:
Explore
The demo draws a random pedigree under a hidden mode of inheritance. Click a mode to test it. If the mode is consistent, the demo shows one set of genotypes that fits everyone (– means either allele) and draws the obligate carriers half-filled. If it is ruled out, the parents and child that make it impossible are ringed in red. The demo assumes full penetrance and no new mutations; people who married in may be carriers.



E1. Test all four modes on the first pedigree. Which are ruled out? For each, write the trio that breaks it, in the form “II-1 × II-2 → III-3”.
E2. Two modes are consistent. Under each, which people must be carriers? Which of them married into the family? Which mode do you favour, and why? Note the double line: does it change your mind? Then press reveal true mode.
E3. Press new pedigree once. Which mode is ruled out now, and by which trio? Of the three modes left, which is most likely? Look at the children of the affected men I-1 and III-3. Under autosomal dominant inheritance, how likely is that pattern?
E4. Press new pedigree about ten times, and test AR each time. How often is AR ruled out? Using the rule-out table, explain why AR is so hard to rule out.
E5. The demo assumes full penetrance. Sketch a small autosomal dominant family that the demo would wrongly rule out as AD if one person in it were non-penetrant. Which of the demo’s verdicts would change?






Solutions: Explore





E1. The pedigree is seed 2. AD is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3 (an affected son of two unaffected parents), and again by III-4 × III-5 → IV-4. XD is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3: an affected son needs XA from his mother, and II-2 is unaffected. The same holds for III-5 → IV-4.
E2. AR and XR are consistent.

Under AR, II-1 and II-2 (the parents of III-3) and III-4 and III-5 (the parents of IV-4) must be carriers. II-1 married into the family, so AR needs a second, unrelated carrier of the same rare allele.
Under XR, I-2, II-2, II-3 and III-5 must be carriers. They are all blood relatives, linked through women, so nobody who married in needs to be a carrier.

XR needs fewer coincidences, so it is favoured. The double line (III-4 and III-5 are first cousins) is a classic hint for AR, and it does explain IV-4 under AR. But it does not explain III-3, whose parents are not related. The true mode is X-linked recessive: affected males related through unaffected women.
E3. (Seed 3.) XR is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (and → III-2): II-2 is an affected woman, so under XR she is XaXa and every son must be affected. AR, AD and XD remain. AR needs two people who married in (II-1 and III-4) to be carriers, so it is unlikely. I-1 has two affected daughters and one unaffected son; III-3 has an affected daughter and an unaffected son. That is exactly the XD pattern. Under AD, each of these five children independently has a ½ chance of matching it: (½)5 = 1/32. XD is the best explanation, and reveal confirms it. One affected son or one unaffected daughter of an affected father would have ruled XD out.
E4. AR is ruled out only rarely. The only trio that excludes it is two affected parents with an unaffected child, because aa × aa can only give aa. Any unaffected person can be a carrier, so an affected child of unaffected parents, or a skipped generation, never contradicts AR. This is why the second step of the strategy (count the carriers a mode needs) matters so much for AR.
E5. For example: I-1 affected, his son II-1 unaffected (but non-penetrant, Aa), and II-1’s daughter III-1 affected, with an unaffected mother II-2. The trio II-1 × II-2 → III-1 is “affected child, both parents unaffected”, so the demo rules out AD, and XD as well, even though the true mode is AD. AR would stay consistent (II-1 and II-2 as carriers). A real geneticist would treat II-1 as an obligate carrier with incomplete penetrance. This is a limit of any rule-out table that assumes full penetrance.

title: Exercise: pedigree analysis
text:
In R
This unit’s new R idiom is simulation with rbinom and replicate, then filtering. rbinom(n, size, prob) draws n binomial random numbers: with size = 1 each draw is 1 (affected) with probability prob, otherwise 0. replicate(N, expr) runs expr N times and collects the results; here each run is one family. We then keep only some families with filter, as a clinic does without meaning to. Use set.seed so that your numbers match the solutions.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Risk as a function
R1. Write a function p_child_affected(p_carrier_mother, p_carrier_father) that returns the probability that a child is affected by an autosomal recessive disease. Check it on two known carriers (answer ¼). Then use it for B6: an unaffected sister of a PKU patient and a man from a population with carrier frequency 1/50. Also compute B7 (both partners have an affected sibling).
p_child_affected <- function(p_carrier_mother, p_carrier_father) {
  p_carrier_mother * p_carrier_father * 1/4
}

p_child_affected(1, 1)          # two known carriers
p_child_affected(2/3, 1/50)     # unaffected sib of a patient x person from the population
1 / p_child_affected(2/3, 1/50) # as "1 in ..."
p_child_affected(2/3, 2/3)      # both partners have an affected sib
R2. The carrier frequency depends on the population. Compute the risk from R1 for carrier frequencies 1/25, 1/50 and 1/100 in one tibble. Your function works on whole vectors, so no loop is needed.
tibble(carrier_freq = c(1/25, 1/50, 1/100)) |>
  mutate(risk = p_child_affected(2/3, carrier_freq),
         one_in = round(1 / risk))


Simulating families
R3. Simulate 10 000 families with Aa × Aa parents and three children each. rbinom(3, size = 1, prob = 1/4) is one family; replicate makes 10 000 of them, one per column. What fraction of all children are affected? How many families have 0, 1, 2 and 3 affected children?
set.seed(1)
n_fam <- 10000
n_kids <- 3
q <- 1/4
kids <- replicate(n_fam, rbinom(n_kids, size = 1, prob = q))
dim(kids)        # 3 rows (children) x 10000 columns (families)
kids[, 1:5]      # the first five families: 1 = affected
mean(kids)       # fraction of all children who are affected

families <- tibble(family = 1:n_fam, n_affected = colSums(kids))
families |> count(n_affected)
R4. A clinic only sees families that have at least one affected child. Keep only those families. What fraction of their children are affected? Compare with the analytic value \(\frac{nq}{1-(1-q)^n}\) affected per family, divided by \(n\).
clinic <- families |> filter(n_affected >= 1)
nrow(clinic)
sum(clinic$n_affected) / (n_kids * nrow(clinic))   # fraction affected among their children

expected_per_family <- n_kids * q / (1 - (1 - q)^n_kids)
expected_per_family
expected_per_family / n_kids
R5. Make a bar chart that compares the fraction of affected children in all families and in the clinic’s families, with a dashed line at the Mendelian ¼.
summary_tbl <- bind_rows(
  families |> mutate(group = "all families"),
  clinic   |> mutate(group = "families with >= 1 affected")
) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n_families = n(),
            frac_affected = sum(n_affected) / (n_kids * n()))
summary_tbl

ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = group, y = frac_affected)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f97", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1/4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(frac_affected, 3)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "fraction of children affected",
       title = "Aa x Aa sibships of 3: ascertainment raises the affected fraction") +
  ylim(0, 0.5)
R6. Does the bias grow or shrink with family size? Compute the analytic fraction \(\frac{q}{1-(1-q)^n}\) for \(n = 1, \dots, 6\). Explain the value for \(n = 1\).
sizes <- 1:6
round(q / (1 - (1 - q)^sizes), 3)

Solutions: By hand





B1. Pedigree A.

AR: consistent. II-1 and II-2 are both carriers.
AD: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (and → III-3): affected children of two unaffected parents.
XR: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1: an affected daughter (XaXa) needs Xa from her father, but II-2 is unaffected.
XD: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (affected daughter of two unaffected parents) and → III-3 (affected son of an unaffected mother).

Only autosomal recessive remains. An affected daughter of unaffected parents is enough on its own.
B2. (a) II-1 and II-2, the parents of the affected children. (b) III-2 is an unaffected child of Aa × Aa: 2/3. (c) II-2 is Aa, so one of his parents is a carrier. If exactly one of I-1 and I-2 is Aa (and the other AA), each of their children is a carrier with probability 1/2. So II-3 is a carrier with probability 1/2.
B3. Pedigree B.

AD: ruled out, for example by I-1 × I-2 → II-3 (affected son of unaffected parents), and again by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 and II-4 × II-5 → III-4.
XD: ruled out by I-1 × I-2 → II-3: an affected son needs an affected mother.
XR: consistent. Carriers needed: I-2, II-2, II-4, all blood relatives; nobody who married in.
AR: consistent. Carriers needed: I-1, I-2, II-2 and II-4, and also II-1 and II-5, who married in. Two unrelated people from outside the family would both have to carry the same rare allele.

XR is most likely: only males are affected, and they are related through unaffected women. Duchenne muscular dystrophy and haemophilia A are inherited like this.
B4. (a) Under XR, II-4 is an obligate carrier (XAXa), and II-5 is XAY. III-5 gets XA from her father and either X from her mother: carrier with probability 1/2. (b) Her son is affected only if she is a carrier and passes Xa: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
B5. Pedigree C.

XR: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3: II-2 is an affected woman (XaXa), so every son should be affected, but III-3 is not. Also II-5 × II-6 → III-5, and II-1 × II-2 → III-4 (affected daughter, unaffected father).
XD, AD and AR are consistent. Ranking:

XD is most likely. The affected father I-1 has both daughters affected and both sons unaffected, exactly as XD predicts. The affected mothers pass it to about half of their sons and daughters, which also fits.
AD fits, but the pattern among I-1’s children is a coincidence under AD: (½)4 = 1/16.
AR needs I-2 and two people who married in (II-1 and II-6) all to be carriers, which is very unlikely for a rare allele.


To rule out XD, find an affected father with an unaffected daughter or an affected son (whose mother is unaffected).
B6. (a) II-2 is an unaffected child of two obligate carriers: 2/3. (b) 2/3 × 1/50 × 1/4 = 2/600 = 1/300. (c) An affected child proves that both parents are Aa. So the risk for the next child is 1/4. Each child is an independent event, and the earlier child does not change the next one.
B7. Each is an unaffected sibling of a patient, so each is a carrier with probability 2/3: 2/3 × 2/3 × 1/4 = 4/36 = 1/9.
B8. (a) Each child of the carrier grandfather is a carrier with probability 1/2. Each grandchild then gets the allele with probability 1/2. So each cousin is a carrier with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. (b) 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64 ≈ 0.016. (c) 1/4 × 1/50 × 1/4 = 1/800 ≈ 0.00125. Marrying a cousin raises the risk about 12.5-fold here, because the allele is in the family. In a random family, where nobody is known to be a carrier, the absolute risk is much smaller.
B9. (a) Her brother is XaY and got Xa from their mother, who is therefore an obligate carrier (XAXa). The woman got one of her mother’s two X chromosomes: carrier with probability 1/2. (b) 1/2 (she is a carrier) × 1/2 (she passes Xa to the son) = 1/4.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
About this lecture
In the 1850s and 1860s, Gregor Mendel crossed garden peas and counted the offspring. From the numbers alone he deduced that inheritance works through discrete factors (we now say genes), present in pairs, that separate cleanly when gametes form.

Mendel’s experimental design: true-breeding lines, controlled crosses, reciprocal crosses, seven clear-cut traits.
The monohybrid cross: P → F1 → F2, the 3 : 1 phenotype ratio and the 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio.
The law of segregation, and why meiosis makes it true.
The testcross, to read an unknown genotype.
The dihybrid cross (9 : 3 : 3 : 1), the law of independent assortment, and its basis in meiosis.
Shortcuts for many genes: the branch-line method, the product rule, and counting 3^n genotypes and 2^n gametes.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, Mendel’s principles of heredity chapter.

This is the foundation of the whole of Part 1. Students have seen Punnett squares at school, so the risk is that they think they already know it. The new things today are the reasoning (how Mendel got from counts to a model), the link to meiosis (why the rules hold), and the shortcuts for several genes. Keep two simplifications in view and name them: complete dominance (the Extensions to Mendel unit relaxes it) and unlinked genes (the Linkage unit in Part 2 relaxes it). Testing whether observed numbers fit a ratio, the chi-square test, is the next unit.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
Why peas? Mendel’s experimental design







Design choice
Why it mattered




True-breeding lines: each line, when self-fertilised for generations, gave only one form of the trait
Mendel knew exactly what each parent would pass on


Controlled crosses: remove the anthers of one flower, dust its stigma with pollen from another
He chose both parents; peas normally self-fertilise, so nothing else got in


Reciprocal crosses: round ♀ × wrinkled ♂ and wrinkled ♀ × round ♂
Same result both ways, so it does not matter which parent gives which form


Either/or traits: round or wrinkled, never “medium”
Offspring can be sorted into classes and counted


Large numbers and several generations
Ratios become visible above the noise



Mendel’s real innovation was quantitative: he counted, and he looked for ratios.

The point of this slide is that the design made the answer possible. Before Mendel, the dominant idea was blending inheritance: offspring are an average of the parents, like mixing paint. Blending predicts that variation should disappear over generations, which it does not. Mendel avoided the traps others fell into by starting from pure lines, by controlling pollination, and by counting. The reciprocal crosses showed that the egg and the pollen contribute equally, which is not obvious and is not true for every trait (sex-linked genes in Part 2, mitochondrial genes in Part 5). Keep the emphasis on counting: this is the link to the chi-square test in the next unit and to the R part of today’s exercise.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
The monohybrid cross
Follow one trait through three generations.


P: true-breeding round × true-breeding wrinkled.
F1: all round. Wrinkled seems to have vanished, but…
F2 (F1 self-fertilised): wrinkled comes back, in about a quarter of the seeds.


The surprise is the F2. Under blending, wrinkled should be gone for good once it was “diluted” in the F1. Instead it comes back unchanged: the F2 wrinkled seeds are just as wrinkled as the original parent. So the wrinkled factor must have been present in the F1, hidden but intact. A monohybrid cross is a cross between parents that differ in one trait, or, equivalently, a cross between two individuals heterozygous for one gene (the F1 x F1 step). Mendel did the same for all seven traits and got the same pattern each time.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
Mendel’s model
Mendel explained the numbers with five ideas. In modern words (recap of the vocabulary from Genetics as information):

Each trait is controlled by a gene, which comes in alternative forms, alleles: R (round) and r (wrinkled).
Each plant carries two alleles of the gene, one from each parent. RR and rr are homozygous; Rr is heterozygous.
In Rr, the dominant allele R decides the phenotype; r is recessive. So RR and Rr look the same.
Each gamete carries one allele, chosen at random: an Rr plant makes ½ R and ½ r gametes.
Fertilisation combines gametes at random.

The genotype is the pair of alleles (Rr). The phenotype is what you see (round).

These five points are the whole model; everything else today follows from them. Point 4 is the key one and gets its own name on the next slides: the law of segregation. Point 5 is what makes the Punnett square work: each cell is equally likely because gametes meet at random. Stress the notation: italics for alleles and genotypes, upper case for the dominant allele, the same letter for both alleles of one gene. R_ (R blank) means “at least one R”, that is RR or Rr, and is the usual shorthand for the dominant phenotype.

Why one third and two thirds and not one quarter and one half? Because we have already removed the rr quarter: among the three quarters that are round, RR is 1/4 out of 3/4, that is 1/3. title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
section: The law of segregation, explained by meiosis
text:
The law of segregation, explained by meiosis

Law of segregation. The two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) during gamete formation, so each gamete gets one of them, with equal probability.


The two alleles sit on the two homologous chromosomes. In meiosis I the homologues go to opposite poles, so an Aa cell gives ½ A and ½ a gametes.

Mendel knew nothing about chromosomes; his law was an inference from counts. About 35 years later Sutton and Boveri noticed that chromosomes in meiosis behave exactly like Mendel’s factors: they come in pairs, the pairs separate, and each gamete gets one of each pair. That is the chromosome theory of inheritance, which is the next block of the course. Walk through the figure: the A allele is on one homologue (blue), a on the other (red). After DNA replication each homologue is two sister chromatids. Meiosis I separates the homologues, meiosis II the sister chromatids. Four gametes, two A and two a. Half and half is not a statistical tendency of the cell; it is built into the mechanics.

text:
The testcross
A round plant can be RR or Rr. How do you tell them apart? Cross it to the homozygous recessive (rr):

The rr parent only gives r gametes, so it hides nothing: each offspring’s phenotype shows directly which allele came from the unknown parent.
A single wrinkled offspring proves that the unknown parent is Rr. Many round offspring and no wrinkled ones make RR likely, but never certain: with n offspring from an Rr parent, the chance that all are round is (½)n.

The testcross is the workhorse of genetic analysis in plants, flies and mice. The trick is that the tester contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring’s phenotypes are a direct readout of the gametes of the unknown parent. That is why testcross ratios are so clean: 1:1 for one gene, 1:1:1:1 for two unlinked genes. We will use exactly this logic in Part 2 to measure recombination: a testcross counts the gamete types directly. Note the asymmetry: one recessive offspring proves heterozygosity, but all-dominant offspring only make homozygosity likely. With 5 offspring the chance of no wrinkled ones from an Rr parent is 1/32, about 3 percent.

text:
The dihybrid cross
Now follow two traits at once: seed shape (R/r) and seed colour (Y yellow / y green).
P: RR YY (round yellow) × rr yy (wrinkled green) → F1: all Rr Yy (round yellow) → selfed:

Mendel’s 556 F2 seeds: 315 : 108 : 101 : 32, close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

A dihybrid is heterozygous for two genes. Mendel asked whether the two traits are inherited as a package (round always going with yellow, as in the parent) or separately. If they travelled together, the F1 would make only RY and ry gametes and the F2 would be 3 round yellow to 1 wrinkled green, with no new combinations. Instead he saw four classes, including two new combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) that neither P parent had. The Punnett square has 16 equally likely cells because each F1 makes 4 gamete types in equal proportions. The expected counts are 556 x 9/16 = 312.75 and so on; Mendel’s numbers fit very well.

So 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is just (3 : 1) × (3 : 1): ¾ × ¾ = 9/16, ¾ × ¼ = 3/16, ¼ × ¾ = 3/16, ¼ × ¼ = 1/16.

Law of independent assortment. Alleles of different genes go into gametes independently of each other. An Rr Yy plant makes RY, Ry, rY and ry gametes, ¼ each.


This is the key insight: the dihybrid ratio is the product of two monohybrid ratios. Whether a seed is round tells you nothing about whether it is yellow. That is exactly what “independent” means in probability, and it is why we can multiply: P(round and yellow) = P(round) x P(yellow). The product rule gets a proper treatment in the next unit, but it is already doing all the work here. Independent assortment is a statement about gametes: all four combinations are equally frequent. The 9:3:3:1 among offspring is a consequence of that plus random fertilisation plus dominance.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
Independent assortment, explained by meiosis

Genes on different chromosomes: at metaphase I each homologue pair lines up independently of the other. Both orientations are equally likely, so the four gamete types are equally frequent: ¼ RY, ¼ ry, ¼ Ry, ¼ rY.
Warning: this needs the two genes to be on different chromosomes (or far apart on the same one). Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and do not assort independently. That is Part 2 of the course.

Walk through the two panels. Blue chromosomes came from the round yellow parent, red ones from the wrinkled green parent. In orientation 1 both blue chromosomes go to the same pole, giving the parental combinations RY and ry. In orientation 2 they go to opposite poles, giving the new combinations Ry and rY. Each cell does one or the other, with equal probability, and across the millions of meioses in a plant the four types come out equal. This is the chromosomal reason for Mendel’s second law. Mendel was lucky, or careful: his seven traits behave as if unlinked. Peas have seven chromosome pairs, but some of his genes do share a chromosome; they are far enough apart that crossing over makes them assort almost independently. The full story of linkage and crossing over is Part 2.

title: Mendel: segregation & assortment
text:
The branch-line method
A Punnett square for two genes has 16 cells; for three genes, 64. The branch-line (forked-line) method is faster: treat each gene separately, then multiply along each branch.

It works because the genes assort independently: each gene contributes its own ratio, and the product rule combines them.

Draw this on the board from left to right. The first column is the monohybrid result for seed shape, three quarters and one quarter. Each branch then splits by seed colour, again three quarters and one quarter. Multiply along each path to get the probability of that combination. Four paths, four phenotypes, the same 9:3:3:1 as the 16-cell square. The method scales: a third gene adds a third column and doubles the number of paths. It also works for genotypes (1/4, 1/2, 1/4 on each branch) and for crosses where each gene has a different parental genotype, for example Aa x aa for one gene and Bb x Bb for the other.

Bring the abstract crosses back to people. Families often believe that “one in four” means that after one affected child the next three are safe. Pedigree analysis, including how to infer the mode of inheritance from a family tree, is its own unit later in Part 1.

Where this leads

Next: Probability & the χ² test. We said “close to 3 : 1” many times. The χ² goodness-of-fit test (chisq.test in R) tells us whether a deviation like 5474 : 1850 is ordinary sampling noise.

title: Quiz: extensions to Mendel
text:
Short questions on dominance, multiple alleles, lethal alleles, penetrance and epistasis. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. For the two-gene questions, start from the 16 squares of a dihybrid Punnett square: 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb.

Q1. Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give an all-pink F₁. What phenotypes, in what ratio, do you expect in the F₂? Why does this show that the parental alleles did not blend?






Hint





With incomplete dominance, each genotype has its own phenotype. What is the genotype ratio of an F₂?









Answer





1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The F₁ is CRCW, and the F₂ genotypes are 1 CRCR : 2 CRCW : 1 CWCW. With incomplete dominance the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio. Red and white come back unchanged in the F₂, so the alleles stayed separate in the pink F₁. Only the phenotype of the heterozygote was intermediate.




Q2. What is the difference between incomplete dominance and codominance? Give one example of each.






Hint





Is the heterozygote an average of the two homozygotes, or does it show both of them?









Answer





In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate (pink snapdragons, from red × white). In codominance the heterozygote shows both parental phenotypes in full (blood type AB: IAIB red cells carry both A and B antigens). In both cases the F₂ phenotype ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.




Q3. A mother has blood type A and a father has blood type B. Their first child has type O. What are the parents’ genotypes, and what is the probability that their next child has type AB?






Hint





A type O child is ii. Where did each i come from?









Answer





The child is ii, so each parent carries i: the mother is IAi and the father IBi. The next child gets IA from the mother with probability 1/2 and IB from the father with probability 1/2, so P(AB) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. (The four blood types A, B, AB and O are equally likely from this cross.)




Q4. Most loss-of-function alleles are recessive. Explain why, and name two ways in which a mutant allele can still be dominant.






Hint





How much protein does a heterozygote make, and is that usually enough?









Answer





A heterozygote for a null allele still makes about half the normal protein, and for most genes that is enough for a normal phenotype (the gene is haplosufficient). A mutant allele can be dominant through any of:

haploinsufficiency: half the protein is not enough;
dominant negative: the mutant protein spoils the normal protein, for example in a dimer or a collagen triple helix;
gain of function: the mutant protein is over-active or does something new, as with FGFR3 in achondroplasia.





Q5. A protein works as a dimer. A heterozygote makes normal and dominant-negative subunits in equal amounts, and they pair at random. What fraction of the dimers is fully normal? Compare with a heterozygote for a null allele that makes no protein.






Hint





Each subunit in a dimer is normal with probability 1/2. Use the product rule.









Answer





A dimer is fully normal only if both subunits are normal: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. A null heterozygote makes only normal subunits, at half the amount, so it has 1/2 of the normal amount of working dimer. The dominant-negative allele does more damage than losing the gene altogether. (For a tetramer, the fraction would be (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.)




Q6. Yellow mice crossed with yellow mice give 2 yellow : 1 agouti, never 3 : 1. Explain. What would you expect from yellow × agouti?






Hint





Which genotype class of a 1 : 2 : 1 is missing?









Answer





All yellow mice are AYa. Yellow × yellow gives 1 AYAY : 2 AYa : 1 aa, but AYAY embryos die. The survivors are 2 yellow : 1 agouti. AY is dominant for coat colour and recessive for lethality (pleiotropy). Yellow × agouti (AYa × aa) gives 1 yellow : 1 agouti, with no deaths, because no AYAY offspring can form.




Q7. A dominant allele causes a disorder with 80% penetrance. A heterozygous parent and a homozygous normal parent have a child. What is the probability that the child is affected?






Hint





Two things must both happen: the child must inherit the allele, and the allele must show.









Answer





P(inherits the allele) = 1/2. P(affected | has the allele) = 0.8. P(affected) = 1/2 × 0.8 = 0.4. So 40% of children are affected and 10% carry the allele without showing it, which is how a dominant trait can skip a generation.




Q8. What is the difference between dominance and epistasis?






Hint





How many genes are involved in each?









Answer





Dominance is a relation between two alleles of the same gene: which allele’s phenotype shows in the heterozygote. Epistasis is a relation between two different genes: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of the other gene (as ee hides B/b in Labrador coat colour).




Q9. Two pure-breeding white-flowered sweet pea lines are crossed. The F₁ is all purple. The F₁ is selfed and gives 9 purple : 7 white. Explain with a pathway, and give the genotypes of the two white parents.






Hint





Which of the 16 squares are purple? What must the F₁ have that neither parent has?









Answer





Colour needs two steps in a row, enzyme A and then enzyme B (colourless → colourless → purple). Only A_B_ plants (9/16) make pigment. A_bb, aaB_ and aabb are all white (3 + 3 + 1 = 7). The parents were AAbb and aaBB. Each lacks a different enzyme, so the F₁ AaBb has both and is purple: the two white mutations complement each other.




Q10. In summer squash, WwYy × WwYy gives white, yellow and green fruit in 12 : 3 : 1. Which genotypes are green, and which gene is epistatic?






Hint





Which class of 16ths is the “1”?









Answer





Green is the 1/16 class, wwyy. Yellow is wwY_ (3/16). Everything with at least one W is white (W_Y_ + W_yy = 9 + 3 = 12). The dominant W allele is epistatic to Y/y (dominant epistasis). Y only shows its effect in ww plants.




Q11. An F₂ from a dihybrid cross has 151 plants with triangular seed capsules and 9 with ovoid capsules. Which ratio would you test first, and why?






Hint





Convert to 16ths: count ÷ total × 16.









Answer





The total is 160. In 16ths: 151/160 × 16 = 15.1 and 9/160 × 16 = 0.9. So test 15 : 1 (duplicate genes): only aabb lacks the product. Expected counts are 150 and 10, and χ² = 1²/150 + 1²/10 = 0.107, df = 1, p ≈ 0.74, which fits. (This is the shepherd’s purse pattern.)




Q12. A dihybrid F₂ has three phenotype classes in 9 : 3 : 4. A student says: “9 : 7 also fits, with p = 0.6, so both models are fine.” What is wrong with this?






Hint





How do you get 9 : 7 from 9 : 3 : 4?









Answer





9 : 7 is 9 : 3 : 4 with the “3” and the “4” merged. If the finer ratio fits, the coarser one will usually fit too, because merging classes throws information away. But you can see three phenotypes, and 9 : 7 predicts only two. A model has to explain every phenotype class you can tell apart. So 9 : 3 : 4 is the answer, and χ² alone cannot make that choice for you.

(a) What is the probability that the man carries the allele? (Hint: use the fact that he is unaffected.) (b) What is the probability that their first child has extra digits?
B6. (recessive epistasis) In Labradors, B_ gives black and bb brown (chocolate) pigment, but ee dogs are yellow whatever their B genotype. (a) Give the F₂ phenotype ratio from BbEe × BbEe, and explain it with a pathway. (b) A black dog is crossed with a yellow bbee dog. Their pups are 3 black, 2 chocolate and 5 yellow. What is the genotype of the black dog? (c) Can two yellow Labradors have a black pup? Explain.
B7. (complementary genes) Two pure-breeding white-flowered sweet pea lines, W1 and W2, are crossed. All F₁ plants are purple, and the F₂ has 9 purple : 7 white. (a) Give the genotypes of W1, W2 and the F₁. (b) What fraction of the white F₂ plants would breed true if selfed (give only white offspring)? (c) A third white line, W3, crossed with W1 gives only white F₁ plants. What does that tell you about the mutation in W3?
B8. (identify the ratio) Summer squash plants from a dihybrid cross give an F₂ of 205 white, 52 yellow and 15 green fruit. (a) Express the counts in 16ths and suggest a ratio. (b) Test it with χ² by hand. (c) Draw a pathway that explains the ratio, and say which genotypes give green fruit.
B9. (dominant suppression and duplicate genes) (a) White Leghorn chickens (CCII) are crossed with White Wyandottes (ccii). C is needed for coloured feathers, and I suppresses colour. What are the F₁ and F₂ phenotypes? (b) A dihybrid F₂ gives 15 : 1 for triangular : ovoid seed capsules. What ratio would an F₁ test cross give, and why can a test cross not separate 15 : 1 from 13 : 3?

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Explore
The demo shows the 16 squares of AaBb × AaBb coloured by phenotype, next to the pathway that explains the colours. Click a square to see which enzymes that genotype has and how far down the pathway it gets.



E1. In recessive epistasis 9 : 3 : 4, click aaBB, then aabb. Both are yellow. Which enzyme is missing in each, and why does the B genotype not matter? Which class of 16ths has merged with which?
E2. Switch to complementary 9 : 7. Click AAbb and aaBB (the two white parents) and then AaBb (their F₁). Explain why two white parents can give a purple F₁. How many different genotypes are white?
E3. Compare dominant epistasis 12 : 3 : 1 with dominant suppression 13 : 3. In both, A_ switches an inhibitor on. Click aabb in each. Why is aabb a class of its own in one preset and merged with white in the other?
E4. Go through all six presets and, for each one, write down which of the four classes A_B_, A_bb, aaB_, aabb are merged. Check your answers against the table in the Background.
E5. In duplicate genes 15 : 1, how many of the 16 squares have no working enzyme? How many have exactly one kind of working enzyme? Why would a geneticist who knocked out only gene A see no phenotype?






Solutions





E1. aaBB lacks enzyme A, so the yellow precursor is never turned into brown, and enzyme B has nothing to work on. aabb lacks both enzymes. Both stop at yellow. The B genotype only matters if step A happens, so aa hides B/b: aa is epistatic. The 3 aaB_ and the 1 aabb merge into 4.
E2. AAbb has enzyme A but not B; aaBB has B but not A. Both are white. The F₁ AaBb gets a working A from one parent and a working B from the other, so both steps work and it is purple: the two mutations complement each other. White squares: AAbb, Aabb, aaBB, aaBb, aabb, which are 5 genotypes in 7 of the 16 squares.
E3. In dominant epistasis, the inhibitor blocks the first step (white → green). aabb has no inhibitor, so it makes green, but it has no enzyme B to make yellow: it stays green, a class of its own (1/16). In dominant suppression, the pathway has only one step, done by enzyme B. aabb has no inhibitor but also no enzyme B, so it is colourless, like the inhibited plants: 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.
E4. None merged: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Recessive epistasis: aaB_ + aabb. Complementary: A_bb + aaB_ + aabb. Dominant epistasis: A_B_ + A_bb. Dominant suppression: A_B_ + A_bb + aabb. Duplicate: A_B_ + A_bb + aaB_.
E5. Only 1 square (aabb) has no working enzyme. Squares with only enzyme A are the 3 A_bb, and squares with only enzyme B are the 3 aaB_: 6 squares have exactly one kind. An aa knockout still has enzyme B (if it is B_), which makes the product on its own. Redundant genes have to be knocked out together before a phenotype appears.

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Find it
F1. The ABO gene. Open NCBI Gene and search for ABO[sym] AND human[orgn]. Open the ABO entry. In the Summary box, read the Location field and the full gene name. On which chromosome is ABO, and in which cytogenetic band? What kind of enzyme does the gene encode, according to its name?
F2. A disease with incomplete penetrance. Open MedGen and search for hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome. Open the entry with that name. Read the Mode of inheritance field. Then open the BRCA1 gene in NCBI Gene and read Location. The OMIM entry for the BRCA1-related disease is MIM 604370 (Breast-ovarian cancer, familial, susceptibility to, 1). Does everyone who inherits a pathogenic BRCA1 variant get cancer? What word from the lecture describes this?
F3. Achondroplasia. Open the MedlinePlus Genetics page on achondroplasia and read the Causes and Inheritance sections. Then check the mode of inheritance in MedGen (entry Achondroplasia). OMIM: MIM 100800. (a) What is the mode of inheritance, and which gene is involved? (b) About what fraction of people with achondroplasia have parents of average height? What does that tell you about where their allele came from? (c) What happens to a child who inherits two altered copies? Which idea from the lecture is this? (d) Is the altered protein less active or more active than normal? Which molecular kind of dominance is it?
F4. Where is FGFR3? In NCBI Gene, read the Location of human FGFR3. Is it on the same chromosome as ABO?






Solutions





F1. NCBI Gene → search ABO[sym] AND human[orgn] → ABO (Gene ID 28) → Summary. Location: 9q34.2, so chromosome 9, long arm (q), band 34.2. The full name is “ABO, alpha 1-3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase and alpha 1-3-galactosyltransferase”: a glycosyltransferase. The A allele adds N-acetylgalactosamine and the B allele galactose to the H antigen, which is why A and B are codominant.
F2. MedGen → Hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome (concept C0677776) → Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. NCBI Gene BRCA1 (Gene ID 672): Location 17q21.31. Not everyone who carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant develops cancer: they inherit a raised risk, not the disease itself. This is incomplete penetrance. (We do not ask for a penetrance number, because the estimates differ between studies and change over time.)
F3. (a) Autosomal dominant; gene FGFR3 (MedlinePlus Inheritance section; MedGen Achondroplasia, C0001080: “Autosomal dominant inheritance”). (b) About 80% of people with achondroplasia are born to parents of average height. Their FGFR3 allele is a new (de novo) mutation, usually arising in a parent’s germ line. (c) Children with two altered copies have a severe form, with very short bones and a small rib cage; they are usually stillborn or die soon after birth. The allele is dominant for short stature and recessive lethal, like AY in mice. (d) MedlinePlus: the variants “cause the FGFR3 protein to be overly active”. This is a gain-of-function allele.
F4. NCBI Gene → FGFR3 (Gene ID 2261) → Location 4p16.3: chromosome 4, short arm. Not the same chromosome as ABO (9q34.2).

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
In R
New idiom today: apply one function to every element of a list. You write a function once, put the hypotheses in a named list, and let purrr::map_dbl() (or base R sapply()) call the function for each hypothesis. map_dbl(xs, f) returns a numeric vector, one value per element of xs, named like xs. Inside map_dbl() you can write a short function as \(h) ..., where h is one element of the list.
The data. data/labrador_f2.csv has coat colours of 384 Labrador pups from matings between black BbEe parents. This is an invented teaching dataset, shaped like pooled kennel records. The recorder split the yellow pups into “fox red” and “cream”, because she wondered if the shade was a third Mendelian class. (In real yellow Labradors the shade varies a lot and is not explained by B or E: this is variable expressivity.)
R1. Load the data and look at it. Add a column with each count expressed in 16ths. Which ratio do the 16ths suggest?
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

f2 <- read_csv("data/labrador_f2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
f2
f2 |> mutate(sixteenths = round(16 * count / sum(count), 2))
R2. Write two functions: chisq_stat(obs, ratio), which returns the χ² statistic for observed counts obs and a ratio such as c(9, 3, 4), and chisq_p(obs, ratio), which returns the p-value with df = number of classes − 1 (use pchisq() with lower.tail = FALSE). Check chisq_p(obs, c(9, 3, 3, 1)) against chisq.test().
obs <- setNames(f2$count, f2$coat)   # a named vector: black, chocolate, fox red, cream

chisq_stat <- function(obs, ratio) {
  expected <- sum(obs) * ratio / sum(ratio)
  # ... return the chi-square statistic
}
chisq_p <- function(obs, ratio) {
  # ... use chisq_stat() and pchisq()
}
R3. Each hypothesis says which recorded classes belong together and what the ratio is. group gives, for each of the four recorded classes (black, chocolate, fox red, cream), the number of the class it belongs to under that hypothesis. tapply() adds up the counts within each group. Use map_dbl() to compute χ² and p for every hypothesis, and collect them in a tibble sorted by p. Then get the same p-values with sapply().
collapse <- function(obs, group) tapply(obs, group, sum)

hypotheses <- list(
  "9:3:3:1" = list(group = c(1, 2, 3, 4), ratio = c(9, 3, 3, 1)),
  "9:3:4"   = list(group = c(1, 2, 3, 3), ratio = c(9, 3, 4)),
  "9:7"     = list(group = c(1, 2, 2, 2), ratio = c(9, 7)),
  "12:3:1"  = list(group = c(1, 1, 2, 3), ratio = c(12, 3, 1)),
  "15:1"    = list(group = c(1, 1, 1, 2), ratio = c(15, 1))
)
collapse(obs, hypotheses[["9:3:4"]]$group)   # black, chocolate, all yellow

results <- tibble(
  hypothesis = names(hypotheses),
  df    = map_int(hypotheses, \(h) length(h$ratio) - 1L),
  chisq = map_dbl(hypotheses, \(h) chisq_stat(collapse(obs, h$group), h$ratio)),
  p     = map_dbl(hypotheses, \(h) chisq_p(collapse(obs, h$group), h$ratio))
) |>
  arrange(desc(p))
results
Which hypotheses are rejected at α = 0.05? Two hypotheses fit. Which one would you choose, and why?
R4. Make a tibble of observed and expected counts for the best-fitting ratio, 9 : 3 : 4 (black, chocolate, yellow), and plot them side by side with pivot_longer() and geom_col(position = "dodge").
R5. (yellow mice) Yellow × yellow mice gave 118 yellow and 62 agouti pups (invented counts). Put the two hypotheses 2:1 and 3:1 in a named list and use your chisq_stat() and chisq_p() with map_dbl() to test both. Which fits? What does that tell you about AYAY?

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Pink × pink (CRCW × CRCW): 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. (b) Pink × white (CRCW × CWCW): 1 pink : 1 white. (c) Red × white (CRCR × CWCW): all pink. Cross (c) gives the most pink seed (100%), and since pink plants do not breed true you must make this cross every season.
B2. The mother is IAIB and the father ii. (a) The child gets IA or IB from the mother (1/2 each) and i from the father: 1/2 type A (IAi) and 1/2 type B (IBi). (b) Neither O nor AB is possible: every child gets exactly one of IA or IB from the mother, and i from the father.
B3. Albino offspring (cc) mean both parents carry c. A chinchilla parent cchc × a Himalayan parent chc gives 1/4 cchch (chinchilla), 1/4 cchc (chinchilla), 1/4 chc (Himalayan), 1/4 cc (albino) = 1/2 chinchilla : 1/4 Himalayan : 1/4 albino. The parents are cchc and chc.
B4. (a) AYa × AYa gives 1/4 AYAY, which die: 1/4 of the zygotes. (b) The survivors are 2 AYa : 1 aa: 2/3 yellow. (c) Yellow × agouti (AYa × aa) gives 1/2 AYa and 1/2 aa, with no deaths. If 8 live pups are 3/4 of the zygotes, a litter starts from about 8 / (3/4) ≈ 10.7 zygotes, so yellow × agouti litters are about 4/3 times as large (≈ 10.7 pups instead of 8).
B5. (a) Before we know his phenotype, P(carrier) = 1/2 (affected father is heterozygous; mother is +/+). Then use the fact that he is unaffected: P(unaffected and carrier) = 1/2 × 0.3 = 0.15; P(unaffected and not carrier) = 1/2 × 1 = 0.5. P(carrier | unaffected) = 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.5) = 0.15 / 0.65 ≈ 0.23. (b) P(child affected) = P(man carrier) × P(passes it on) × penetrance = 0.23 × 1/2 × 0.7 ≈ 0.081, about 8%.
B6. (a) 9 black (B_E_) : 3 chocolate (bbE_) : 4 yellow (B_ee + bbee). Pathway: E_ is needed to put dark pigment in the hair at all; B_ makes that dark pigment black rather than brown. ee stops the pathway before B matters, so ee is epistatic to B. (b) Chocolate pups (bbE_) mean the black parent carries b; yellow pups (ee) mean it carries e. So the black dog is BbEe, and this is a test cross: expected 1 black : 1 chocolate : 2 yellow, close to 3 : 2 : 5 in a litter of 10. (c) No. Yellow dogs are ee, so all their pups are ee and yellow (whatever their B genotype; their noses may differ).
B7. (a) W1 = AAbb, W2 = aaBB (or the other way round), F₁ = AaBb. (b) White F₂ plants: 1 AAbb, 2 Aabb, 1 aaBB, 2 aaBb, 1 aabb (7/16). Every one of them lacks a working copy of at least one gene for good: A_bb plants are bb, so all their offspring are bb and white; aaB_ plants are aa, so all offspring are white; aabb likewise. So all 7/7 white F₂ plants breed true for white. (c) W3 × W1 gives a white F₁, so W3 does not complement W1: the W3 mutation is in the same gene as W1’s (gene B if W1 is AAbb).
B8. (a) Total = 272. In 16ths: 205/272 × 16 = 12.06, 52/272 × 16 = 3.06, 15/272 × 16 = 0.88. Suggests 12 : 3 : 1 (dominant epistasis). (b) Expected: 272 × 12/16 = 204, 272 × 3/16 = 51, 272 × 1/16 = 17. χ² = (205 − 204)²/204 + (52 − 51)²/51 + (15 − 17)²/17 = 0.0049 + 0.0196 + 0.2353 = 0.26, df = 2. Since 0.26 < 5.99, do not reject; p ≈ 0.88. (For comparison, 9 : 3 : 4 in the same order gives χ² ≈ 46.8, clearly rejected.) (c) White precursor → (step 1) → green → (enzyme from Y) → yellow, and the dominant W allele blocks step 1. W_ is white; wwY_ is yellow; wwyy is green.
B9. (a) F₁ CcIi: white (I suppresses colour). F₂: coloured only if C_ii (3/16); C_I_ (9), ccI_ (3) and ccii (1) are white: 13 white : 3 coloured. (b) F₁ test cross AaBb × aabb gives AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Under 15 : 1 only aabb lacks the product: 3 triangular : 1 ovoid. Under 13 : 3 (coloured only aaBb) the test cross is also 3 : 1. Both merge three of the four test-cross classes, so the test cross cannot tell them apart; only the F₂ (15 : 1 vs 13 : 3) can.









Solutions: In R





R1. The 16ths are about 8.8 : 3.2 : 2.2 : 1.9. Black and chocolate look like 9 and 3, but fox red and cream are close to 2 and 2, not 3 and 1. Together they make 4.0, which suggests 9 : 3 : 4.

title: Quiz: genetics as information
text:
Short questions on the vocabulary and ideas of the first lecture. Try each one on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is the difference between a gene, an allele and a locus? Use HBB and sickle-cell disease in your answer.






Hint





One is an address, one is what lives there, and one is a version of it.









Answer





The locus is the position on the chromosome (for HBB, band 11p15.4 on chromosome 11). The gene is the DNA sequence at that position that encodes a product (HBB, encoding β-globin). An allele is one version of the gene: HbA (normal) and HbS (sickle) are two alleles of HBB.




Q2. A person has the genotype HbA/HbS. Are they homozygous or heterozygous at HBB? How many different HBB alleles can one person carry at most, and why?






Hint





How many copies of chromosome 11 does a body cell have?









Answer





Heterozygous: the two alleles differ. One person carries at most two alleles at an autosomal locus, because a diploid cell has two copies of each autosome, one from each parent. A population can contain many more alleles than two.




Q3. “Huntington disease is caused by a dominant allele, so it must be common.” What is wrong with this statement?






Hint





Does dominance say anything about how many people carry the allele?









Answer





Dominance describes what the heterozygote looks like: if Aa shows the same phenotype as AA, then A is dominant. It says nothing about the frequency of the allele in the population. The Huntington allele is dominant and rare. Allele frequencies are a question for population genetics.




Q4. In sickle-cell disease, one base change in HBB changes codon 6 from GAG to GTG. Which amino acid change does this cause, and why does it make the haemoglobin behave differently?






Hint





Look up GAG and GTG in the genetic code. One of the two amino acids is charged, the other hydrophobic.









Answer





GAG codes for glutamate (Glu, negatively charged) and GTG for valine (Val, hydrophobic). The valine sits on the surface of the protein and makes a sticky patch, so deoxygenated HbS molecules stick together into long fibres that distort the red cell into a sickle shape.




Q5. Is the sickle allele HbS dominant, recessive or codominant to HbA? Explain why there is more than one correct answer.






Hint





Compare the heterozygote with the two homozygotes for (a) disease, and (b) the types of haemoglobin found in the blood.









Answer





For the disease, HbS is recessive: HbA/HbS carriers are usually healthy, and only HbS/HbS has the disease. For the haemoglobin protein, the alleles are codominant: a heterozygote makes both HbA and HbS, and both appear on a gel. Dominance is defined for one phenotype at a time, so the answer depends on which phenotype you look at.




Q6. A database search lists HBB with the organism “Homo sapiens”, and Hbb-bs with “Mus musculus”. Why is one written in capitals and the other not? Are they the same gene?






Hint





Gene naming conventions differ between species. “Same gene” in two species has a technical name.









Answer





Human gene symbols are written all in capitals; mouse symbols have only the first letter capitalised. Both are β-globin genes, but because the β-globin cluster has duplicated separately in different mammal lineages, the mouse genes do not pair one-to-one with human HBB. Genes in different species that descend from one ancestral gene are orthologs; for HBB the relationship is complicated by duplications (paralogs). For a clean one-to-one example, see human CFTR and mouse Cftr.




Q7. The human genome is about 3,100 Mb with about 20,000 protein-coding genes. The axolotl genome is about 29,000 Mb with about 24,000 protein-coding genes. Compute the genes per Mb for each. What explains the difference?






Hint





Divide genes by Mb. Then think about what fills the rest of a large genome.









Answer





Human: \(20{,}000 / 3{,}100 \approx 6.5\) genes per Mb. Axolotl: \(24{,}000 / 29{,}000 \approx 0.8\) genes per Mb, about eight times fewer. The axolotl does not have many more genes; its genome is larger because it has more non-coding DNA, mostly repeated sequences such as transposable elements, and very long introns. This is the C-value paradox: genome size does not follow gene number or complexity.




Q8. Why can we learn about a human disease gene by studying a mouse, a zebrafish or even a fly?






Hint





What is an ortholog, and what tends to happen to the function of a gene over evolution?









Answer





Many genes are conserved: the human gene has an ortholog in the model organism that descends from the same ancestral gene and often has a similar function. For example, human CFTR and mouse Cftr are one-to-one orthologs whose proteins are about 79% identical. Model organisms can be crossed, mutated and studied in ways that are impossible in humans, and the results often carry over.




Q9. Which of the four approaches (transmission, molecular, genomic, population) is each study using?

Counting how many children of two carriers have sickle-cell disease.
Sequencing HBB to find the GAG→GTG change.
Comparing the frequency of HbS in regions with and without malaria.
Comparing the whole genomes of human and mouse to find shared genes.







Hint





Ask what is being measured: offspring of crosses, one gene’s DNA or protein, whole genomes, or allele frequencies in groups.









Answer






Transmission (inheritance in families). b. Molecular (one gene’s DNA). c. Population (allele frequencies in groups). d. Genomic (whole genomes).





Q10. A fly with white eyes carries two copies of the mutant allele w. The normal red-eyed allele is written w+. What does the “+” mean, and what does the name of the white gene tell you about how it was discovered?






Hint





Is the white gene needed to make white eyes or red eyes?









Answer





The “+” marks the wild-type allele, the standard allele in laboratory stocks. The gene is named after its mutant phenotype: it was found because flies lacking a working copy had white eyes. The working gene is in fact needed to make red eyes.

title: Exercise: genetics as information
Exercise: genetics as information
Exercise: genetics as information
text:
Background
Recap from 5MO103. Information flows DNA → RNA → protein → phenotype. A gene is a DNA segment that encodes a functional product. Its position on a chromosome is its locus.
Vocabulary.

An allele is one version of a gene. A diploid individual carries two alleles at each autosomal locus.
Genotype: the alleles carried, e.g. AA, Aa, aa. Phenotype: what is observed or measured.
Homozygous: two identical alleles. Heterozygous: two different alleles.
Wild type (w+): the standard allele in a lab population. Mutant: a changed allele.
If Aa has the same phenotype as AA, then A is dominant and a is recessive for that phenotype. In this unit we assume complete dominance; Extensions to Mendel adds the other cases.

Sickle-cell disease. The human gene HBB (chromosome 11) encodes β-globin. In the sickle allele HbS, codon 6 changes from GAG to GTG, and glutamate (Glu) becomes valine (Val). Databases count the start methionine too, so they write this change as c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val.
Genomes. Genome size (in megabases, Mb = 106 bp) varies more than 10,000-fold across life, but the number of protein-coding genes varies far less. Most of a large genome is non-coding: introns, intergenic DNA, repeats such as transposable elements. Some genomes are also large because of polyploidy.
Orthologs are genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor. Paralogs arise by duplication within one genome.

title: Exercise: genetics as information
text:
In R
The data for this part is in data/genomes.csv (download it and put it in a data/ folder next to your script). It lists ten organisms with genome size and protein-coding gene count. Every value comes from the NCBI Datasets reference genome and its current annotation, and the source column gives the assembly accession for each row.
New idiom: log-scale axes and text labels. When values span many orders of magnitude (here 4.6 to 29,118 Mb), a linear axis squashes most points into a corner. scale_x_log10() and scale_y_log10() space the axis by powers of ten instead, so 10, 100 and 1,000 are equally far apart. geom_text(aes(label = ...)) writes a label at each point, so you can see which organism is which without a legend.
R1. Build the table. Create the tibble with tribble() (one row per line, easy to read) and save it with write_csv(). If you downloaded the CSV, you can skip straight to R2, but read the code so you know where each number came from.

  "Homo sapiens",             "human",         "animal",     3099.4,   20054, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000001405.40 (RefSeq annotation 2026-11)",

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

R3. Genes per Mb. Add a column genes_per_mb with mutate(), then show it sorted from densest to least dense genome with arrange(desc(...)). Check the E. coli, yeast and human values against your answer to B6.

  mutate(genes_per_mb = protein_coding_genes / genome_mb)

  select(common_name, genome_mb, protein_coding_genes, genes_per_mb) |>

Hint B3: counting codons and nucleotides





Write the sequence in triplets and number the codons 1, 2, 3, … from ATG. Codon n covers nucleotides \(3n-2\) to \(3n\). So nucleotide 20 is in codon 7 (nucleotides 19–21). Codon 7 counting the Met is amino acid 6 without the Met.

Find the node in the tree where two genes last shared an ancestor. If that node is a speciation (the human–mouse split), the genes are orthologs. If it is a duplication, they are paralogs.
