title: Exercise: genetics as information
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a. w+/w+: homozygous, red eyes. b. w+/w: heterozygous, red eyes (w+ is dominant). c. w/w: homozygous, white eyes. w+ is the wild type; w is the mutant.
B2. “HBB is a gene at a locus on chromosome 11. HbA and HbS are two alleles of it. A person with the genotype HbS/HbS has the phenotype sickle-cell disease.”
B3. a. ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GAG GAG AAG → Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Glu Glu Lys. b. Without Met: Val(1) His(2) Leu(3) Thr(4) Pro(5) Glu(6) Glu(7) Lys(8). Amino acid 6 is glutamate. c. Nucleotides 19–21 are codon 7 (GAG), so nucleotide 20 is the A in the middle of GAG. A→T gives GTG, which codes for Val. The protein becomes Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Val Glu Lys. Traditional name: Glu6Val; database name: c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val (the same change, counted with the Met).
B4. c.19 is the first base of codon 7 (GAG). G→A gives AAG, which codes for Lys. The change is p.Glu7Lys (traditionally Glu6Lys). This is the haemoglobin C allele; ClinVar lists NM_000518.4(HBB):c.19G>A (p.Glu7Lys).
B5. Disease row: the heterozygote looks like HbA/HbA, so HbS is recessive for disease. Gel row: the heterozygote shows both bands, so the alleles are codominant for the haemoglobin protein. It is not a contradiction because dominance is a statement about one phenotype. Each allele makes its own protein (codominance at the protein level), but half normal haemoglobin is enough to avoid disease under normal conditions (recessive at the level of disease).
B6. a. E. coli: \(4{,}290 / 4.6 \approx 933\) genes per Mb. Yeast: \(6{,}021 / 12.1 \approx 498\). Human: \(20{,}054 / 3{,}099.4 \approx 6.5\). b. \(20{,}054 / 933 \approx 21.5\) Mb, which is less than 1% of the real 3,099 Mb. c. Introns, large intergenic regions, and repeated sequences (especially transposable elements), plus centromeres, telomeres, regulatory DNA and genes for non-coding RNAs.
B7. a. The tree has a duplication node at the root (G → G1, G2). Below each of G1 and G2 is a speciation node (human, mouse). b. Orthologs: human G1–mouse G1, and human G2–mouse G2 (they last shared an ancestor at the speciation). Paralogs: human G1–human G2, mouse G1–mouse G2, and also human G1–mouse G2 and human G2–mouse G1 (their last common ancestor is the duplication). c. The mouse would have a single gene G. Both human G1 and human G2 would be orthologs of mouse G: a one-to-many (in Ensembl, “1-to-many”) orthology. Human G1 and G2 would be paralogs of each other. This is roughly what has happened in the β-globin cluster, which is why there is no simple 1-to-1 mouse ortholog of human HBB.
B8. a. Transmission, human families (a pedigree or family study). b. Molecular/transmission genetics in yeast: a fast, single-celled organism where thousands of mutants can be screened. (A genomic screen, testing every gene, also fits.) c. Molecular, in the mouse: knock out the Cftr ortholog and look at the phenotype. The mouse is a mammal with lungs and a gut similar to ours. d. Population, in humans: compare HbS allele frequencies between populations.









Solutions: Find it





All facts checked in November 2026 (NCBI Gene; Ensembl release 116 on GRCh38; Alliance of Genome Resources).
F1. NCBI Gene, HBB. Click path: NCBI Gene → search HBB human → row HBB, Homo sapiens → Gene ID 3043. a. Official full name: hemoglobin subunit beta. b. Gene ID: 3043. c. Chromosome 11. d. Location 11p15.4: “p” is the short arm of chromosome 11 (“q” is the long arm), and 15.4 is the band (region 1, band 5, sub-band 4) counted outwards from the centromere. HBB lies near the tip of the short arm. e. Also known as: beta-globin (other aliases listed are CD113t-C and ECYT6). The gene has 3 exons.
F2. Ensembl, HBB. Click path: Ensembl → Human → HBB → Go → HBB (Human Gene) → ENSG00000244734. a. ENSG00000244734. b. Chromosome 11: 5,225,464–5,229,395, reverse strand (GRCh38). The gene is read from right to left on the standard chromosome map. c. In release 116 the transcript table lists 19 transcripts (most protein-coding, some “nonsense mediated decay” or “retained intron”). Your number may differ in a later release, which is why we note the release. Many extra transcripts come from new long-read evidence; most of the protein is made from one main transcript. d. HBB-201 (ENST00000335295) is the MANE Select and Ensembl canonical transcript. It matches RefSeq NM_000518.5 and encodes 147 aa (146 aa in the mature chain, after the start Met is removed).
Optional observation: if you open Orthologues for HBB, Ensembl lists orthologs in many species, but no mouse gene. The β-globin genes duplicated separately in the primate and rodent lineages, so mouse Hbb-bs and Hbb-bt do not pair one-to-one with human HBB (compare B7c). That is why F3 uses CFTR for the mouse ortholog.
F3. CFTR. a. Click path: NCBI Gene → CFTR human → Gene ID 1080. Chromosome 7, location 7q31.2 (long arm). Official full name: CF transmembrane conductance regulator (the older name “cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator” is still widely used). b. Click path: Ensembl → Human → CFTR → ENSG00000001626 → Comparative Genomics → Orthologues → Mouse. The mouse gene is Cftr (ENSMUSG00000041301). Type: 1-to-1. Target %id: about 79% (78.7% in release 116), meaning about 79% of the mouse protein’s amino acids are identical to the aligned human ones. c. Mouse Cftr is on mouse chromosome 6 (GRCm39). Chromosome numbers are not shared between species.
F4. Alliance of Genome Resources. Click path: alliancegenome.org → search CFTR → CFTR (Homo sapiens, HGNC:1884) → Orthology. a. With the stringent default filter, only vertebrates are listed: zebrafish cftr, mouse Cftr, rat Cftr, and frog (Xenopus tropicalis cftr; X. laevis cftr.L and cftr.S). b. With no filter, many fly and yeast genes appear: in fly a gene actually named Cftr, plus Mrp4, Mrp5, Sur and several CG-numbered genes; in yeast YOR1, YCF1, STE6, YBT1 and others. Each is supported by only one or two prediction methods (e.g. Ensembl Compara, PANTHER), against about ten for the mouse ortholog. c. Fly and yeast have related ABC-transporter genes, the same protein family as CFTR, but no high-confidence one-to-one ortholog. Gene families are conserved across all eukaryotes; a specific member like CFTR may only be clearly traceable among vertebrates.

R6. Example answer: Genome size varies more than 6,000-fold in this table, but gene number only about 25-fold, and among animals 290-fold against 2-fold. Large genomes are not large because they have more genes, but because they have more non-coding DNA: long introns, large intergenic regions and especially repeated sequences such as transposable elements. Polyploidy (wheat) adds whole extra genomes, and with them extra gene copies. So the amount of DNA (the C-value) says little about the number of genes or the complexity of the organism.

title: Glossary
text: A running glossary of the genetics, database and statistics terms used in this course. Definitions are kept short, and each one links to the unit where the term is introduced.

title: Glossary
text:
Part 1: Mendelian genetics

Genes and genomes
Allele: one version of a gene. Alleles differ in DNA sequence. See Genetics as information.
C-value paradox: genome size does not follow gene number or organism complexity, because most of a large genome is non-coding DNA. See Genetics as information.
Dominant / recessive: if Aa has the same phenotype as AA, then A is dominant and a is recessive, for that phenotype. See Genetics as information.
Gene: a DNA segment that carries the information for one functional product, usually a protein. See Genetics as information.
Genotype: the alleles an individual carries at a locus, e.g. Aa. See Genetics as information.
Hemizygous: having only one copy of a gene, as males do for genes on the X chromosome. See Pedigree analysis.
Homozygous / heterozygous: carrying two identical alleles, or two different alleles, at a locus. See Genetics as information.
Locus: the position of a gene on a chromosome. See Genetics as information.
Model organism: a species that is easy to grow and cross, used because many of its genes are shared with other species. See Genetics as information.
Ortholog: genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor. See Genetics as information.
Paralog: genes related by a duplication within one genome. See Genetics as information.
Phenotype: an observable or measurable trait, from a disease to a protein band on a gel. See Genetics as information.
Wild type: the standard allele or phenotype in a lab population, written with a +, e.g. w+. See Genetics as information.


Mendel’s crosses
Branch-line (forked-line) method: solving a multi-gene cross one gene at a time, then multiplying the probabilities along each branch. See Mendel.
Dihybrid cross: a cross between individuals heterozygous for two genes (AaBb × AaBb). It gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypes when the genes are unlinked. See Mendel.
Law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes enter gametes independently, because homologue pairs orient independently at metaphase I. It holds for unlinked genes. See Mendel.
Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, ½ each, because homologues separate in meiosis I. See Mendel.
Monohybrid cross: a cross between individuals heterozygous for one gene (Aa × Aa). It gives 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes and 3 : 1 phenotypes. See Mendel.
Punnett square: a grid of one parent’s gametes against the other parent’s gametes. Each cell is one equally likely fertilisation. See Mendel.
Reciprocal cross: the same cross done both ways round, to test whether it matters which parent carries the allele. See Mendel.
Testcross: a cross to a homozygous recessive individual. The offspring phenotypes show the other parent’s gametes directly. See Mendel.
True-breeding line: a line that gives only offspring like itself when self-fertilised, because it is homozygous. See Mendel.


Probability and the χ² test
Binomial distribution: the probability of k outcomes of one kind in n independent trials, (n choose k) pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. It is used for family composition. See Probability & the χ² test.
χ² goodness-of-fit test: a test of whether observed counts fit the counts expected from a hypothesised ratio, using χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. See Probability & the χ² test.
Conditional probability: the probability of an event given that another event is known to have happened. For example, P(carrier | unaffected child of Aa × Aa) = 2/3. See Probability & the χ² test.
Critical value: the χ² value that is exceeded with probability 0.05 under H0 (3.84 for df = 1). See Probability & the χ² test.
Degrees of freedom (df): the number of counts that are free to vary once the total is fixed. It is k − 1 for k classes and a ratio given in advance. See Probability & the χ² test.
Fail to reject: the outcome when p ≥ 0.05. The data are consistent with H0, but this does not prove H0. See Probability & the χ² test.
Null hypothesis (H0): the hypothesis being tested, here a Mendelian ratio such as 3:1. Expected counts are computed assuming it is true. See Probability & the χ² test.
p-value: the probability, if H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that H0 is true. See Probability & the χ² test.
Product rule: the probability that independent events all happen is the product of their probabilities, e.g. P(aabbcc) = (¼)³. See Probability & the χ² test.
Sum rule: the probability that one of several mutually exclusive events happens is the sum of their probabilities. See Probability & the χ² test.


Extensions to Mendel
Codominance: the heterozygote shows the phenotypes of both alleles in full, as in blood type AB (IAIB). See Extensions to Mendel.
Complementary genes: two genes that are both needed for a phenotype, giving a 9 : 7 F₂ ratio. See Extensions to Mendel.
Dominant negative: a mutant protein that interferes with the normal protein from the other allele, for example in a dimer. See Extensions to Mendel.
Duplicate genes: two redundant genes, where one working copy of either is enough, giving a 15 : 1 F₂ ratio. See Extensions to Mendel.
Epistasis: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene. This changes the dihybrid 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio into ratios such as 9 : 3 : 4 or 9 : 7. See Extensions to Mendel.
Expressivity: how strongly a phenotype shows in the individuals who have it. See Extensions to Mendel.
Haploinsufficiency: one working copy of a gene does not make enough product for a normal phenotype, so a loss-of-function allele is dominant. See Extensions to Mendel.
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote’s phenotype lies between those of the two homozygotes, so the F₂ phenotypes are 1 : 2 : 1, as in snapdragon flower colour. See Extensions to Mendel.
Multiple alleles: more than two alleles of a gene exist in a population, as in the ABO blood group. See Extensions to Mendel.
Penetrance: the fraction of individuals with a given genotype who show the expected phenotype at all. See Extensions to Mendel.
Pleiotropy: one gene or allele affecting several different traits. See Extensions to Mendel.
Recessive lethal allele: an allele that kills homozygotes. Among the survivors of a heterozygote cross this gives a 2 : 1 ratio, as for the yellow mouse allele AY. See Extensions to Mendel.


Pedigrees
Ascertainment bias: distortion of observed ratios caused by the way families are found, for example only through an affected child. See Pedigree analysis.
Consanguinity: a mating between related people, drawn as a double line. It raises the risk of recessive disease. See Pedigree analysis.
Male-to-male transmission: a trait passed from father to son. It rules out X-linked dominant inheritance and makes X-linked recessive inheritance unlikely. See Pedigree analysis.
Obligate carrier: an unaffected person who must be heterozygous because of where they are in the pedigree, for example a parent of a child with a recessive disease. See Pedigree analysis.
Pedigree: a family tree drawn with standard symbols that shows who is affected by a trait and how they are related. See Pedigree analysis.
Proband: the affected person through whom a family first comes to attention, marked with an arrow. See Pedigree analysis.


Databases
ClinVar: the NCBI database that links human variants to clinical interpretations. Each record has a classification and a review status. See Pedigree analysis.
HGVS notation: the standard naming of variants, e.g. c.1222C>T (coding DNA) and p.Arg408Trp (protein). See Pedigree analysis.
MIM number: the six-digit identifier of a gene or disease entry in OMIM. See Pedigree analysis.

title: Basic and molecular genetics
text:
Topics

Part 1: Mendelian genetics. Genes and alleles, Mendel’s laws, probability and the χ² test, extensions to Mendel (dominance, lethality, epistasis, penetrance), and pedigree analysis.
More parts follow the course book: chromosomes and mapping, DNA and mutation, genome analysis, chromosomes in detail, gene regulation and development, and population and complex-trait genetics.

See Canvas for the most up-to-date study instructions.

title: Genetics as information
text:
About this lecture
Genetics is the study of biological information: how it is stored in DNA, how it is copied and passed on, and how differences in it become differences between individuals.

A short recap of DNA → RNA → protein → phenotype (from 5MO103).
The words we will use all course: gene, allele, locus, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, wild type, mutant, dominant, recessive.
One gene followed all the way from DNA to disease: HBB and sickle-cell disease.
Genomes differ hugely in size, but many genes are shared. That is why model organisms work.
Four ways to study genetics, which are also a map of this course.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, introductory chapter (“Genetics: the study of biological information”).

This is the orientation lecture. Nothing here is hard, but almost every later unit leans on the vocabulary, so the aim is precision rather than depth. Say clearly that the molecular part is a recap from 5MO103 and that we will not re-teach transcription or translation; what is new is the genetic way of looking at it: we care about how differences in DNA become differences in phenotype. The sickle-cell example will come back several times in the course (dominance, pedigrees, population genetics), so it is worth setting it up carefully today.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genetics is about information
Recap from 5MO103. The information in DNA is copied into RNA and read into protein. Proteins do the work that we see as the phenotype.


DNA is the store: it is replicated and passed to the next generation.
RNA and protein are the readout: they are made fresh in each cell.
The genetic question is about differences: a change in the DNA can change the protein, which can change the phenotype.


Keep this brief: students have seen the central dogma in detail in 5MO103. The new emphasis is the last bullet. A geneticist almost never studies a gene by itself; we study a difference (a variant, a mutation) and ask what difference it makes. That comparative mindset is what unites Mendel’s crosses with modern genome sequencing. Point out that “function” on the last arrow hides a lot of biology (metabolism, development, environment), which is why one gene rarely maps simply to one trait; we simplify today and return to it in Extensions to Mendel and Complex traits.

title: Genetics as information
text:
What is a gene?
A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries the information for one functional product, usually a protein (sometimes only an RNA).

A gene has a position on a chromosome. Human HBB, for example, sits on chromosome 11.
A gene is named with a symbol in italics: HBB (human), Cftr (mouse), w (white, fly).
The protein is written in plain type: the β-globin protein, the CFTR protein.

The definition of “gene” has moved over a century, from Mendel’s abstract “factor” to a DNA sequence. For this course, a working definition is enough: a DNA segment whose product does something. Stress the notation convention now, because students will meet it in every database: gene symbols in italics, human symbols in upper case, mouse symbols with only the first letter capital, fly genes named after their mutant phenotype. Proteins are not italic. This is a small thing that marks the difference between sloppy and professional writing.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genes, alleles and loci


Locus (plural loci): the place on a chromosome where a gene sits.
Allele: one version of a gene. Different alleles differ in DNA sequence.
A diploid organism has two copies of each autosomal locus, one from each parent. So it carries two alleles, which can be the same or different.


The classic confusion is between gene and allele. Use the language: “the gene” is HBB; “the alleles” are the normal version and the sickle version. A population can have many alleles at one locus, but one diploid individual carries at most two. The locus is the address, the gene is what lives at the address, and the alleles are the different versions that can live there. The notation A and a is the Mendelian shorthand; we will use it from the next unit onwards.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genotype and phenotype

Genotype: the alleles an individual carries at a locus, e.g. AA, Aa or aa.
Phenotype: what we can observe or measure: a colour, a disease, an enzyme activity, a protein band on a gel.
Homozygous: two identical alleles (AA or aa). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Aa).

The phenotype depends on the genotype and on the environment. Sickle-cell symptoms, for example, get worse at low oxygen.
The same genotype can be described at different levels of phenotype: the whole organism, the cell, or the protein. We will see that this matters for the word “dominant”.

Phenotype is a much broader word than students expect. It is not only visible traits; a band on a protein gel or the level of an enzyme is also a phenotype. That breadth is important for the sickle-cell example in a few slides, where the “dominance” relationship changes with the level at which we look. Also introduce the environment early: a genotype gives a range of possible phenotypes, and the environment picks one. Homozygous and heterozygous apply to one locus at a time; an individual can be homozygous at one locus and heterozygous at the next.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Wild type and mutant

Wild type: the allele (or phenotype) that is most common in natural or laboratory populations. Written with a plus: w+ in the fly.
Mutant: an allele that differs from wild type, usually because of a mutation, a heritable change in the DNA.
In the fly, the white gene is named after its mutant phenotype: w flies have white eyes, w+ flies have red eyes.

In humans and other natural populations, many loci have several common alleles, and none is the obvious “wild type”. Then we just name the alleles, for example the ABO blood groups.

Wild type is a model-organism idea. It works well in lab stocks of flies, worms or mice, where one standard allele exists. It works less well in humans, where many alleles at a locus are common and calling one of them “normal” is arbitrary. Keep the word mutant neutral: it simply means changed, not harmful. Many mutations have no visible effect at all. The fly white gene is the textbook example of naming genes after the mutant phenotype, which confuses students at first: the white gene is needed to make red eyes.

title: Genetics as information
section: Dominant and recessive: a first pass
text:
Dominant and recessive: a first pass
In a heterozygote Aa:

if Aa looks like AA, then A is dominant and a is recessive;
the recessive phenotype appears only in aa.

Common misunderstandings.

Dominant does not mean common. Huntington disease alleles are dominant and rare.
Dominant does not mean “better” or “stronger”.
Dominance describes the relationship between two alleles for one phenotype. It is not a property of one allele alone.

This is a simplification: complete dominance. Incomplete dominance and codominance come in the Extensions to Mendel unit.

Students come with secondary-school ideas, and the most persistent one is that dominant alleles spread or are common. Kill that early: frequency in the population is a separate question that belongs to population genetics. Also make the point that dominance is a statement about a pair of alleles and a particular phenotype. The sickle-cell example on the next slides shows that the same pair of alleles can be recessive for one phenotype and codominant for another. Flag the simplification honestly and name where the full story comes.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Worked example: sickle-cell disease (1)
The gene. HBB, “hemoglobin subunit beta”, on human chromosome 11 (band 11p15.4).

HBB encodes β-globin. Two β-globin and two α-globin chains make one haemoglobin molecule, which carries oxygen in red blood cells.
The gene is small: 3 exons, about 1.6 kb of DNA.
The normal allele is called HbA. The sickle allele is HbS.

The difference. HbS has one base change: codon 6 is GAG in HbA and GTG in HbS. The amino acid changes from glutamate (Glu) to valine (Val).
You will look HBB up in NCBI Gene and Ensembl in the exercise.

Sickle-cell disease was the first disease explained at the molecular level (Pauling and colleagues in 1949 showed that the haemoglobin was different; Ingram in the 1950s found the single amino-acid change). It is therefore the cleanest possible example of genotype to phenotype. Numbering: the classic name is Glu6Val, which counts amino acids in the mature chain without the initiator methionine. Databases use the HGVS standard, which counts the methionine, so they write p.Glu7Val and c.20A>T. Mention this now so students are not confused when they meet it in ClinVar. All facts on this slide are on the NCBI Gene and Ensembl pages they will open.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Worked example: sickle-cell disease (2)


Walk through the figure from top left. One base (A to T in the coding strand) changes one codon (GAG to GTG) and one amino acid (Glu to Val). Valine is hydrophobic; on the surface of deoxygenated haemoglobin it creates a sticky patch, so HbS molecules polymerise into long fibres when oxygen is low. The fibres bend the red cell into a sickle shape. Sickled cells are stiff, block small vessels, causing pain and organ damage, and are destroyed early, causing anaemia. At the bottom, the three genotypes: two normal alleles, carrier, and two sickle alleles. The carrier state also gives partial protection against severe malaria, which is why HbS is common in regions where malaria is or was common. We return to that in population genetics.

At the protein level, each allele makes its own product. The heterozygote has both.
So “recessive” is a statement about one phenotype, not about the allele itself.


This slide is the payoff of the vocabulary. The disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait; that is how it appears in pedigrees and in OMIM. But a carrier’s red cells can sickle under extreme low oxygen, and on an electrophoresis gel both haemoglobin types are seen side by side, which is codominance. This is not a contradiction; it shows that dominance is defined relative to a phenotype. Students will meet codominance again in the Extensions to Mendel unit, and the electrophoresis view is the cleanest way to understand it. Use this to reinforce that “recessive” does not mean “does nothing” in the heterozygote.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genomes differ hugely in size


Genome: all the DNA of an organism (one copy of each chromosome).
Genome size runs from about 5 Mb (E. coli) to over 29,000 Mb (axolotl).
The number of protein-coding genes is far less variable: about 4,000 to 28,000 in this set.


The numbers come from NCBI Datasets, the reference genome for each species and its current annotation. Gene counts are approximate and change a little with each annotation release, so we round in speech. The key observation: genome size spans almost four orders of magnitude; gene number varies about sevenfold. A human has roughly the same number of protein-coding genes as a mouse or a worm. The axolotl, a salamander, has a genome ten times larger than ours with a similar gene number. Students will plot these exact data in R in the exercise.

title: Genetics as information
text:
The C-value paradox
The C-value is the amount of DNA in one haploid genome. The paradox: C-value does not follow organism complexity or gene number.
Why? Most of a large eukaryotic genome does not code for protein:

introns inside genes, and large intergenic regions;
repeated sequences, especially transposable elements, which can make up most of a genome;
polyploidy: bread wheat has three ancestral genomes, which is why it has so many genes.

Bacteria are the exception. Their genes are packed tightly: E. coli has about 900 genes per Mb, humans about 6.

The C in C-value originally meant constant: each species has a characteristic amount of DNA per haploid nucleus. The paradox was that this amount is not related to complexity: some amphibians and plants have far more DNA than mammals. Today we understand it mainly as differences in non-coding DNA, especially transposable elements, and in polyploidy. It is sometimes called the C-value enigma, because once we know about repeats it is not really a paradox any more. The genes-per-Mb comparison is the R task in the exercise, so do not give away too many numbers; the two quoted here are rounded.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Many genes are shared
Genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor are orthologs. Genes that arose by duplication within a genome are paralogs.

Human CFTR (chromosome 7) and mouse Cftr (chromosome 6) are one-to-one orthologs. Their proteins are about 79% identical (Ensembl).
The zebrafish cftr protein is still about 56% identical to the human one.
HBB is part of a gene family: α-, β-, γ-, δ-globins are paralogs, made by old duplications. Families like this can make one-to-one orthologs hard to define.

Because genes and their functions are conserved, what we learn about a gene in one species often holds in others.

Orthology is the reason comparative genetics works. The identity figures come from the Ensembl Compara orthologue pages (release 116). Mention that the globin family is a nice example of duplication: humans have several β-like globin genes expressed at different developmental stages, and the duplications happened separately in different mammal lineages, so the mouse β-like globins do not pair one-to-one with ours. That is why Ensembl does not list a simple mouse ortholog for HBB, and why the exercise uses CFTR for the mouse ortholog task. Paralogs come back in Genome annotation.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Why model organisms work
A model organism is easy to grow, cross and manipulate, and what we learn in it often applies to other species, because many genes are shared.

The trade-off is between ease and similarity to humans. Yeast and worms are fast and cheap but distant; mice are close but slow and expensive. Most human disease genes have counterparts in mouse, many in fly and fewer in yeast. Generation times are rough, under lab conditions, and vary with temperature and strain; do not let students memorise them, only the order. Mention the community databases: SGD, WormBase, FlyBase, TAIR, ZFIN and MGI, now joined in the Alliance of Genome Resources, which the exercise uses for an optional task.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Four ways to study genetics

These four approaches are also the map of this course. Each one asks a different question about the same information.

Use the figure as a map. Transmission genetics is Mendel’s approach: crosses and pedigrees, inferring genes from patterns of inheritance, without seeing any DNA. Molecular genetics looks at the DNA and its products directly. Genomics looks at whole genomes at once. Population genetics asks how allele frequencies change over generations and between populations. The approaches complement each other: sickle-cell disease was first recognised by transmission (a recessive pattern in families), explained molecularly (Glu to Val), and its frequency explained by population genetics (malaria). Point out where each part of the course sits.

text:
Where this leads

Mendel: alleles segregate into gametes, and we predict genotype ratios in crosses (Aa × Aa).
Extensions to Mendel: incomplete dominance, codominance and the other complications we postponed today.
Gene expression recap and Genome annotation: transcripts, exons and orthologs in more depth.
Hardy–Weinberg and Drift and selection: why HbS is common where malaria is.


Point forward. The next unit starts with Mendel’s peas, which is transmission genetics with no molecular knowledge at all. Ask students to keep the sickle-cell example in mind: every Mendelian rule we learn can be checked against it.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
About this lecture
Mendel picked traits that behave simply: one gene, two alleles, one fully dominant, no interactions, no environment. Most traits are not that tidy. Today we keep Mendel’s two laws (segregation and independent assortment) and change the assumptions about how genotype becomes phenotype.

One gene: incomplete dominance and codominance, why some alleles are dominant at the molecular level, multiple alleles, lethal alleles, pleiotropy, penetrance and expressivity, and the environment.
Two genes: genes acting in the same pathway change the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 into 9 : 3 : 4, 9 : 7, 12 : 3 : 1, 13 : 3 or 15 : 1. These are still 16ths, merged.
Strategy: given an F₂, turn the counts into 16ths, guess which classes merged, then test the guess with χ² (from Probability and the χ² test).

Book: Hartwell, the chapter on extensions to Mendel’s laws.

The key message: the laws of transmission do not change. Alleles still segregate 1:1 and unlinked genes still assort independently. What changes is the mapping from genotype to phenotype. Every odd ratio in this lecture can be derived from an ordinary Punnett square, then relabelled. Students who remember that will never need to memorise the ratios. The χ² test from the previous unit comes back at the end, as the tool for choosing between candidate ratios. Linkage, which breaks independent assortment, is a different story and comes in Part 2.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Dominance is a relation between two alleles
text:
Dominance is a relation between two alleles


Complete dominance: the heterozygote looks like one homozygote (Pp is purple). F₂ phenotypes 3 : 1.
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between. Red × white snapdragons give pink F₁, and the F₂ is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white: phenotype ratio = genotype ratio.
Codominance: the heterozygote shows both phenotypes in full. IAIB red cells carry both A and B antigens: blood type AB.

“Dominant” describes a pair of alleles, not one allele, and not how common it is.

Start from the snapdragon: it is the cleanest way to show that segregation still works perfectly. The F1 is pink, which looks like blending, but the F2 brings back red and white unchanged, in 1:2:1. Blending inheritance would never give back the parental types. In the incomplete-dominance case you can read the genotype straight off the phenotype, so the phenotype ratio is the genotype ratio. Codominance differs from incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is not an average, it shows both products side by side, as A and B antigens on the same red cell. Stress that dominance is a relation: the I-A allele is codominant with I-B but dominant over i. Also the misconception: a dominant allele is not necessarily common; polydactyly alleles are dominant and rare.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Why is an allele dominant? The molecular view
text:
Why is an allele dominant? The molecular view


Most loss-of-function alleles are recessive: half the normal protein is usually enough (haplosufficient).
Haploinsufficiency: half is not enough, so a loss-of-function allele is dominant (e.g. PAX6 and aniridia).
Dominant negative: the mutant protein spoils the normal one in a complex (e.g. mutant collagen chains in osteogenesis imperfecta).
Gain of function: the mutant protein does something new or too much (e.g. an over-active FGFR3 receptor in achondroplasia).


This links the Mendelian words to the molecular biology students know from 5MO103. Ask first: if a mutation destroys an enzyme, why is the heterozygote usually normal? Because one working copy gives about half the enzyme, and pathways usually have spare capacity. So recessive is the default for loss-of-function alleles. Then the three ways around this. Haploinsufficiency: a dosage-sensitive gene, where 50% is below the threshold. Dominant negative: in a dimer, random pairing in a heterozygote leaves only 1/4 of dimers fully normal, which is worse than the 1/2 from a plain null allele; for tetramers it is only 1/16. Gain of function: the mutant protein is active when it should not be. Achondroplasia comes back in Find it: FGFR3 variants make the receptor overly active.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Multiple alleles
A population can carry many alleles of one gene, even though each diploid person carries at most two.
ABO blood groups (gene ABO, which encodes a glycosyltransferase):










Genotype
IAIA, IAi
IBIB, IBi
IAIB
ii




Blood type
A
B
AB
O



IA and IB are codominant with each other; both are dominant over i (no working enzyme). Three alleles give 6 genotypes but 4 phenotypes.
An allelic series: rabbit coat colour, C (full colour) > cch (chinchilla) > ch (Himalayan) > c (albino). Each allele is dominant over those to its right.
With n alleles there are n(n + 1)/2 genotypes: 3 alleles → 6, 4 alleles → 10.

ABO combines two ideas: multiple alleles, and different dominance relations between different pairs. The A allele adds N-acetylgalactosamine and the B allele adds galactose to the same precursor (the H antigen); the O allele makes no active enzyme. So A and B are codominant, both products are present, and O is recessive because it makes nothing. The rabbit series is the textbook allelic series and sets up the Himalayan allele, which comes back on the environment slide. The formula n(n+1)/2 is n homozygotes plus n(n-1)/2 heterozygotes; a quick check of their combinatorics from the probability unit.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Lethal alleles and pleiotropy: the yellow mouse
text:
Lethal alleles and pleiotropy: the yellow mouse


Cuénot (1905): yellow × yellow mice always gave yellow and agouti offspring, in a ratio near 2 : 1, never 3 : 1. Yellow mice never bred true.
The AYAY embryos die. AY is dominant for coat colour but recessive for lethality.
One allele affecting several traits is pleiotropy. Another example: the sickle-cell allele of HBB affects red cell shape, anaemia, organ damage and resistance to malaria.
A 2 : 1 ratio among the survivors of a monohybrid cross is the signature of a recessive lethal.


This is the classic case where a ratio looked wrong and the explanation was a missing class. Ask students to predict yellow x yellow first: they will say 3:1. Then show 2:1 and ask what has happened. The test for the hypothesis: yellow mice are always heterozygous, so yellow x agouti should give 1:1, and pregnant yellow x yellow females should show about a quarter of embryos dying early. Pleiotropy: the same allele has one effect we see (coat colour, dominant) and one we infer (lethality, recessive). That shows again that “dominant” belongs to a trait, not to an allele. In the exercise, students test 2:1 against 3:1 with χ².

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Penetrance and expressivity


Penetrance: the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show the trait at all. Incomplete penetrance can make a dominant trait skip a generation in a pedigree.
Expressivity: how strongly the trait shows in those who have it. Polydactyly can be one small extra digit, or extra digits on all four limbs.
BRCA1: carriers of a pathogenic variant have a much higher lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, but not all of them get cancer. They inherit a raised risk, not the disease.
Causes: other genes (modifiers), the environment, and chance.


Keep the two words apart: penetrance is yes/no at the level of individuals, expressivity is the degree among affected individuals. Penetrance is a fraction of genotypes, so it can only be measured when we know the genotype, which is why molecular testing changed our estimates of penetrance for BRCA1. Do not quote penetrance numbers for BRCA1 here: they differ between studies and populations, and they change. The important qualitative fact is: autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance. In the pedigrees unit, incomplete penetrance is the classic trap: an unaffected parent between two affected generations does not rule out dominant inheritance. In Find it students look up the mode of inheritance in MedGen/OMIM.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
The environment changes the phenotype
The same genotype can give different phenotypes in different environments.

Himalayan rabbits (chch) and Siamese cats carry a temperature-sensitive allele of the gene for tyrosinase, the first enzyme in melanin synthesis.
The enzyme works at lower temperature and fails at body-core temperature, so only the cool extremities (ears, nose, paws, tail) are dark.
Shave a patch on a Himalayan rabbit’s back and keep it cold while the fur regrows: the new fur grows in dark.
In humans, phenylketonuria (PKU): the same genotype gives severe intellectual disability on a normal diet and near-normal development on a low-phenylalanine diet.

Genotype sets a range of possible phenotypes. The environment picks a point in that range.

The rabbit experiment is the cleanest demonstration that the genotype of every skin cell is the same; only the temperature differs. The allele makes a protein that folds correctly at lower temperature. PKU is the human example where knowing the environment lets us change the phenotype: newborn screening plus diet. This leads to the idea of the norm of reaction, which returns with quantitative traits in Complex traits. It also explains part of incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity from the previous slide.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Two genes, one pathway: epistasis
Epistasis: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene. Mendel’s 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is still there underneath; some classes look the same.

Recessive epistasis, 9 : 3 : 4. Labrador retrievers, BbEe × BbEe: ee dogs make no dark pigment in the hair, so they are yellow whatever their B genotype. ee is epistatic to B; B is hypostatic.

Epistasis is about genes, not alleles: one gene masks another. Contrast with dominance, which is about two alleles of the same gene. The pathway picture: a later step only matters if the earlier step happens. Here E is needed for dark pigment in the hair at all, and B decides whether that dark pigment is black or brown. The pathway is simplified: in reality E (MC1R) acts as a switch between dark and yellow pigment, but the logic is the same. Yellow Labradors with bb still show it: their nose and lips are brown rather than black. That is a hint that the B genotype is still there, just hidden in the coat. Point out how 9:3:4 comes from 9:3:3:1 with the last two classes merged: B_ee (3) and bbee (1).

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Complementary genes: 9 : 7
Both steps of the pathway are needed; losing either one gives the same mutant phenotype.
\text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme A}\ } \text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{purple}

Bateson and Punnett (sweet pea): two white varieties crossed gave an all-purple F₁. The F₁ selfed gave 9 purple : 7 white.
The parents were AAbb and aaBB. Each could make what the other could not, so the F₁ AaBb has both enzymes.
Only A_B_ is purple (9). A_bb, aaB_ and aabb are all white (3 + 3 + 1 = 7).
Also called duplicate recessive epistasis: aa hides B, and bb hides A.

Two white parents with a coloured F₁ is the same logic as a complementation test: the mutations are in different genes.

This is the slide that sets up the complementation test in the Mutation unit. When two recessive mutants with the same phenotype are crossed and the offspring are wild type, the mutations are in different genes; they complement. If they were in the same gene, the F1 would still be mutant. Point out the merged classes: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. The pathway explains why: you get purple only if both steps work. Ask students what an F1 test cross AaBb x aabb would give: 1 purple : 3 white.

The W allele (dominant) is epistatic to Y/y. Only ww plants show what the Y gene does.

Now the first two classes merge instead of the last two. The dominant W allele stops pigment production early, so W_ fruit is white whatever Y is. In ww plants the pathway runs: green pigment is made, and Y_ converts it to yellow; yy plants stay green. Compare with recessive epistasis: there the epistatic genotype was the homozygous recessive (ee), here it is any genotype with one dominant allele (W_). That is why the merged class is 12 instead of 4. Test cross: WwYy x wwyy gives 2 white : 1 yellow : 1 green.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Dominant suppression 13 : 3 and duplicate genes 15 : 1


Dominant suppression, 13 : 3
\text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{pigment} A_ makes an inhibitor of enzyme B.

Coloured only if aaB_: 3.
A_B_, A_bb, aabb are colourless: 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.
Chickens: White Leghorn (CCII) × White Wyandotte (ccii) → F₂ 13 white : 3 coloured. I suppresses C.


Duplicate genes, 15 : 1
\text{precursor} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme A}\ \text{or}\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{product}

Two redundant genes do the same job; one working copy of either is enough.
Only aabb lacks the product: 1. All others: 15.
Shepherd’s purse: triangular seed capsules unless aabb (ovoid).



Two more ways to merge classes. In dominant suppression, a dominant allele of one gene makes a suppressor that stops the other gene’s product from acting. Unlike 12:3:1, the double recessive aabb is colourless too, because it lacks enzyme B, so it joins the big class: 13. Make students explain why aabb is white: no inhibitor, but also no enzyme. Duplicate genes are common in plants with genome duplications, such as shepherd’s purse, which is tetraploid. Redundancy is also why many single knockouts in model organisms have no visible phenotype; you need to knock out both copies. Test crosses: 13:3 gives 3 colourless : 1 coloured; 15:1 gives 3 : 1.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Strategy: collapse the F₂ into 16ths

How many phenotype classes? Two classes from a dihybrid cross points to 9 : 7, 13 : 3 or 15 : 1; three classes to 9 : 3 : 4, 12 : 3 : 1 (or 9 : 6 : 1); four to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Convert to 16ths: count ÷ total × 16.
Match to sums of 9, 3, 3, 1. For example 4 = 3 + 1, 7 = 3 + 3 + 1, 12 = 9 + 3, 13 = 9 + 3 + 1, 15 = 9 + 3 + 3.
Test the candidates with χ², with df = number of classes − 1.
Explain it with a pathway, and check with a test cross if you can.

Worked example. Sweet pea F₂: 382 purple, 290 white (672 plants).

382/672 × 16 = 9.1 and 290/672 × 16 = 6.9 → try 9 : 7.
Expected 378 and 294: χ² = 4²/378 + 4²/294 = 0.097, df = 1, p = 0.76. Fits.
Under 3 : 1 instead: χ² = 118, p ≈ 10⁻²⁷. Rejected.


The point of step 2 is that it turns counts into something you can compare with ratio tables at a glance. Students should be able to do steps 1 to 3 in their head. The χ² step is from the previous unit; the only new thing is that we now have several candidate ratios to compare. Note a warning: any ratio that merges classes of a ratio that fits will also fit, because merging throws away information. For example, if 9:3:4 fits, then 9:7 (merge brown with yellow) will usually fit too. Choose the ratio that has the same number of classes as the phenotypes you can actually tell apart. The exercise works through exactly that with R. Worked numbers: (382-378)^2/378 + (290-294)^2/294 = 0.042 + 0.054 = 0.097.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Where this leads

Pedigree analysis (next unit): incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity and new mutations make human pedigrees harder to read.
Mutation and complementation: the 9 : 7 cross is a complementation test. Two recessive mutants that give a wild-type F₁ have mutations in different genes.
Linkage: when two genes are close on a chromosome, the dihybrid classes are no longer 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, for a quite different reason.
Complex traits: many genes and the environment together give continuous variation.


Point forward. The most immediate use is pedigrees, where incomplete penetrance and de novo mutations (achondroplasia: about 80% of cases are new mutations) change how we read a family tree. Complementation is the experimental version of the 9:7 logic. Linkage is the other big reason a dihybrid ratio may not be 9:3:3:1, and students must not confuse it with epistasis: linkage changes the frequency of genotype classes, epistasis changes how genotype classes map to phenotypes. Finally, complex traits extend the environment and modifier ideas to many genes at once.

Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Background
Notation. Each gene has two alleles; upper case is dominant (R, round), lower case is recessive (r, wrinkled). A diploid genotype has two alleles: RR and rr are homozygous, Rr is heterozygous. R_ means “RR or Rr”, that is, the dominant phenotype. Throughout, we assume complete dominance (the Extensions to Mendel unit relaxes this) and unlinked genes (Linkage, Part 2, relaxes this).
Law of segregation. The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, so an Rr plant makes ½ R and ½ r gametes. The reason is meiosis I: the two homologous chromosomes, one carrying R and one carrying r, go to opposite poles.
Law of independent assortment. Alleles of different genes go into gametes independently. An Rr Yy plant makes RY, Ry, rY, ry, ¼ each. The reason: at metaphase I, each homologue pair lines up independently of the others. This holds for genes on different chromosomes.

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
By hand
B1. (monohybrid, peas) In peas, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant to green (y). Mendel crossed a true-breeding yellow line with a true-breeding green line, then selfed the F1.

Give the genotypes of the P plants, the F1 and the F1 gametes.
Draw the Punnett square for the F2 and give the genotype and phenotype ratios.
Mendel counted 8023 F2 seeds. How many yellow and green seeds do you expect? He observed 6022 yellow and 2001 green.

B2. (hidden genotypes) Among the yellow F2 seeds of B1, what fraction are YY and what fraction are Yy? Describe an experiment Mendel could do (and did) to tell them apart without a testcross.
B3. (testcross, mouse) In mice, black coat (B) is dominant to brown (b). A black male is crossed to a brown female.

What offspring do you expect if the male is BB? If he is Bb?
The litter has 4 black and 3 brown pups. What is the male’s genotype?
Another black male sires 6 pups, all black, with brown females. Can you be sure he is BB? What is the probability of this result if he is actually Bb?

B4. (dihybrid, peas) Mendel crossed true-breeding round yellow (RR YY) with wrinkled green (rr yy) peas and selfed the F1.

What gametes does the F1 make, and in what proportions? Which law are you using?
Give the four F2 phenotype classes with their expected fractions.
Mendel counted 556 F2 seeds. Compute the expected number in each class and compare with 315 : 108 : 101 : 32.
Add up the counts for seed shape alone, and for seed colour alone. What ratios do you get?

B5. (dihybrid testcross) The F1 from B4 (Rr Yy) is crossed to a wrinkled green plant (rr yy).

Give the expected offspring phenotypes and their ratio.
Why does the testcross show the F1’s gametes directly?
Suppose instead that R and Y were so close together on one chromosome that they never separated. What would the testcross give?

B6. (branch-line) Use the branch-line method for Rr Yy × Rr yy. Give every phenotype class and its probability.
B7. (product rule, three genes) Tall stem (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Consider Tt Rr Yy × Tt Rr Yy.

How many kinds of gamete does each parent make? How many different genotypes can the offspring have?
What fraction of the offspring is tall, round and green?
What fraction is tt rr yy? What fraction is Tt Rr Yy?
What fraction is dominant for all three traits?

B8. (working backwards) In peas, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p), and axial flowers (A) are dominant to terminal (a). Two plants are crossed, giving offspring in the ratio 3 purple axial : 3 purple terminal : 1 white axial : 1 white terminal. What are the parents’ genotypes?
B9. (humans) Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive; Huntington disease is autosomal dominant.

Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What are the parents’ genotypes? What is the chance that their next child is affected? That their next two children are both unaffected?
An unaffected sister of the affected child wants to know if she is a carrier. What is the probability?
A man with Huntington disease (heterozygous) and an unaffected woman have a child. What is the risk for the child? Which kind of cross is this?

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. In the demo you choose 1 or 2 genes and each parent’s genotype. You see each parent’s gametes with their frequencies, the Punnett square (coloured by phenotype, assuming complete dominance), and the genotype and phenotype ratios. Below, the demo simulates N offspring: filled bars are the observed counts, dashed bars the expected ones. “draw again” gives a new random sample (the seed number goes up by one).



E1. The demo starts on the monohybrid F1 × F1 (Aa × Aa). Check the gametes, the Punnett square and both ratios against your answer to B1. Now set N = 16 and press “draw again” a few times, writing down the number of aa offspring each time. How often do you get exactly the expected 4?
E2. Set N = 1000. Compare the proportion of aa offspring with N = 16 and with N = 1000. In which case is the proportion closer to ¼? Which of Mendel’s seven traits would you expect to deviate most from 3 : 1?
E3. Click “dihybrid F1 × F1”. How many distinct gametes does each parent make, how many cells does the square have, and how many genotypes and phenotypes are there? Switch the bars to “genotypes”: which genotype is the most common, and why?
E4. Click “dihybrid testcross”. Why does the Punnett square have only one row? Compare the four phenotype classes with the gametes of the AaBb parent. Then look at N = 100: are the four classes equal?
E5. Before you click, predict the phenotype ratio of AA Bb × aa bb. Then set it up with the genotype buttons and check.






Solutions: Explore





E1. Each parent makes A and a, ½ each; the square has 4 cells: genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 (¼ AA, ½ Aa, ¼ aa) and phenotypes 3 : 1 (¾ A_, ¼ aa), as in B1. With N = 16, seed 1 gives exactly 12 A_ : 4 aa, but the next draws give 15 : 1 (seed 2) and 13 : 3 (seed 3). Hitting the expected count exactly is the exception, not the rule. A 3 : 1 mechanism does not guarantee a 3 : 1 sample.
E2. At N = 1000 (seed 1) there are 757 A_ : 243 aa, so the proportion of aa is 0.243. At N = 16 the proportion jumped between 1/16 = 0.06 and 4/16 = 0.25 in the first three draws. Larger samples come closer to ¼ in proportion, even though the difference in counts (here 7) can be larger than at N = 16. Among Mendel’s traits, pod colour (580 plants: 2.82 : 1) and stem length (1064 plants: 2.84 : 1) have the smallest samples and deviate most; seed shape and seed colour (7324 and 8023 seeds) are closest to 3 : 1.
E3. Each parent makes 4 gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab, ¼ each), so the square has 4 × 4 = 16 cells. There are 9 genotypes (32), with ratio 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 4 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1, and 4 phenotypes (9 : 3 : 3 : 1). The most common genotype is AaBb (4/16 = ¼): it is heterozygous for both genes, and heterozygous is the most likely outcome for each gene (½ · ½ = ¼).
E4. The aabb parent makes only one kind of gamete (ab), so there is one row. The four cells (AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb) correspond one to one to the four gametes of the AaBb parent (AB, Ab, aB, ab): the testcross reads off the gametes. Expected 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, that is 25 each at N = 100, but seed 1 gives 24 : 18 : 34 : 24. Even at N = 100, a class can be off by 9 by chance.
E5. AA Bb makes AB and Ab gametes (½ each); aa bb makes only ab. Offspring: ½ AaBb (A_B_) and ½ Aabb (A_bb), so the phenotype ratio is 1 : 1, and all offspring show the dominant A phenotype. The square is 2 × 1.

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
In R
In R we simulate crosses. The new idiom is writing your own function and using sample() to draw at random. A function packs a few lines of code under one name, so you can run them again with different inputs:
my_function <- function(input1, input2) {
  # ... code that uses input1 and input2 ...
  result            # the last value is what the function returns
}
sample(x, n, replace = TRUE) draws n values from the vector x at random, with each value equally likely and the same value allowed more than once. That is exactly what a parent does when it passes one of its two alleles to each offspring.
We use set.seed() before each simulation, so you get the same random numbers as in the solutions.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
R1. (two functions) Write gametes(genotype), which splits a genotype like "Aa" into its two alleles, and cross(p1, p2, n), which simulates n offspring of a single-gene cross: each offspring gets one allele drawn at random from each parent.
gametes <- function(genotype) {
  strsplit(genotype, "")[[1]]          # "Aa" -> c("A", "a")
}

cross <- function(p1, p2, n) {
  a1 <- sample(gametes(p1), n, replace = TRUE)   # one allele from parent 1
  a2 <- sample(gametes(p2), n, replace = TRUE)   # one allele from parent 2
  # write the dominant (upper-case) allele first, so "aA" becomes "Aa"
  ifelse(a1 == toupper(a1), paste0(a1, a2), paste0(a2, a1))
}

gametes("Aa")
set.seed(1)
cross("Aa", "Aa", 16)
Count the genotypes in your 16 offspring by eye. Do you get exactly 4 : 8 : 4?
R2. (monohybrid: 1 : 2 : 1 and 3 : 1) Simulate 1000 offspring of Aa × Aa. Use table() and prop.table() to get the genotype counts and proportions, and compare them with 1 : 2 : 1. Then turn genotypes into phenotypes and compare with 3 : 1. Finally, compute the expected numbers for Mendel’s 7324 seeds and his observed ratio.
set.seed(2)
offspring <- cross("Aa", "Aa", 1000)
geno <- factor(offspring, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))   # fixes the order
table(geno)
prop.table(table(geno))

pheno <- ifelse(offspring == "aa", "aa", "A_")
prop.table(table(pheno))

7324 * c(3/4, 1/4)     # Mendel's 7324 seeds, expected round : wrinkled
5474 / 1850
R3. (testcross) Reuse cross() for the testcross Aa × aa with 1000 offspring. What ratio do you expect, and what do you get?
set.seed(3)
tc <- cross("Aa", "aa", 1000)
table(factor(tc, levels = c("Aa", "aa")))
R4. (two genes: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1) Independent assortment means that we can simulate each gene separately and put the results side by side. Simulate 1000 offspring of AaBb × AaBb, build the phenotype of each offspring, count the four classes with count(), and compare the proportions with 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16. Then compute the expected numbers for Mendel’s 556 seeds.
set.seed(44)
n <- 1000
dihybrid <- tibble(A = cross("Aa", "Aa", n),
                   B = cross("Bb", "Bb", n)) |>
  mutate(pheno = paste0(ifelse(A == "aa", "aa", "A_"),
                        ifelse(B == "bb", "bb", "B_")),
         pheno = factor(pheno, levels = c("A_B_", "A_bb", "aaB_", "aabb")))

dihybrid |>
  count(pheno) |>
  mutate(observed = n / sum(n),
         expected = c(9, 3, 3, 1) / 16)

556 * c(9, 3, 3, 1) / 16     # Mendel's 556 seeds
R5. (more offspring, less noise) Write a function prop_aa(n) that simulates one Aa × Aa cross with n offspring and returns the proportion of aa. Run it 20 times for each of n = 16, 160, 1600 and 16000, summarise, and plot the results with ggplot2. sapply() calls a function once for each value in a vector and collects the answers; we meet it again in Part 2.
prop_aa <- function(n) {
  mean(cross("Aa", "Aa", n) == "aa")     # TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0
}
set.seed(5)
sims <- tibble(n = rep(c(16, 160, 1600, 16000), each = 20))
sims$prop_aa <- sapply(sims$n, prop_aa)

sims |>
  group_by(n) |>
  summarise(lowest = min(prop_aa), mean = mean(prop_aa), highest = max(prop_aa))

ggplot(sims, aes(x = n, y = prop_aa)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1/4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(16, 160, 1600, 16000)) +
  labs(x = "number of offspring (log scale)",
       y = "proportion aa",
       title = "20 simulated Aa x Aa crosses for each n") +
  theme_minimal()
How much does the spread shrink each time n grows ten-fold? Where would Mendel’s 7324 seeds sit on this plot?
R6. (three genes: the product rule) Simulate 64000 offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc. Check the fraction that is aa bb cc against 1/64, the fraction dominant for all three traits against 27/64, and count the distinct genotypes (compare with \(3^3\)).
set.seed(6)
n <- 64000

Where this leads
Every simulated cross above was a little off from its expected ratio, and so were all of Mendel’s. In Probability & the χ² test we turn “a little off” into a number: the χ² goodness-of-fit test (chisq.test() in R) asks whether a deviation like 5474 : 1850 against 3 : 1 is the size that chance usually produces. Later, Linkage (Part 2) shows what happens when two genes sit close together on one chromosome and independent assortment fails.

title: Quiz: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Short questions on monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and the two laws. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless the question says otherwise, assume complete dominance and unlinked genes.

Q1. What is a true-breeding line, and why did Mendel need true-breeding parents?






Hint





What happens when a true-breeding plant is self-fertilised? What genotype must it have?









Answer





A true-breeding line gives only offspring like itself when self-fertilised, generation after generation. That means it is homozygous (RR or rr). Mendel needed this so that he knew exactly what each parent passes on: every gamete of a true-breeding round plant carries R. Without that, the F1 and F2 ratios could not be interpreted.




Q2. Mendel crossed round ♀ × wrinkled ♂ and also wrinkled ♀ × round ♂. What are these called, and what did the identical results tell him?






Hint





Which parent supplies the egg, and which the pollen?









Answer





They are reciprocal crosses. Getting the same F1 (all round) either way showed that the egg and the pollen contribute equally to the trait: it does not matter which sex the allele comes from. (This is not always true: sex-linked and mitochondrial genes, later in the course, give different results in reciprocal crosses.)




Q3. In Mendel’s F2 for seed shape there were 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. What are the expected numbers under a 3 : 1 ratio? Does the deviation prove that the model is wrong?






Hint





Total = 5474 + 1850. Multiply by ¾ and ¼.









Answer





Total = 7324. Expected: 7324 × ¾ = 5493 round and 7324 × ¼ = 1831 wrinkled. Observed is 19 fewer round and 19 more wrinkled. A small deviation like this is expected from random sampling: each seed is an independent draw, and a sample of draws almost never matches the probabilities exactly. Whether 19 is “too big” needs a test, the χ² goodness-of-fit test, in the next unit.




Q4. An F2 plant from Rr × Rr has round seeds. What is the probability that it is heterozygous?






Hint





You already know it is not rr. Of the ¾ that are round, how much is Rr?









Answer





Among all F2 plants: ¼ RR, ½ Rr, ¼ rr. Given round, only RR and Rr remain, in a ratio of ¼ : ½ = 1 : 2. So P(Rr | round) = ½ ÷ ¾ = ⅔. Mendel confirmed this: when he selfed 565 round F2 plants, 193 bred true and 372 gave both round and wrinkled offspring, close to 1 : 2.




Q5. State the law of segregation and name the event in meiosis that makes it true.






Hint





Where are the two alleles of one gene in a diploid cell?









Answer





The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets one allele, and each allele goes to half of the gametes. The two alleles sit on the two homologous chromosomes, and in anaphase of meiosis I the homologues move to opposite poles. Every gamete therefore gets one homologue, and so one allele, of each pair.




Q6. A purple-flowered pea plant (purple P is dominant over white p) is crossed to a white-flowered plant. The cross gives 12 purple and 0 white offspring. What is the purple plant’s genotype? How sure can you be?






Hint





This is a testcross. If the purple plant were Pp, what is the chance that all 12 offspring are purple?









Answer





This is a testcross. The result fits PP (all offspring Pp, purple). It does not prove it: if the plant were Pp, each offspring would be purple with probability ½, so all 12 purple has probability (½)12 = 1/4096 ≈ 0.00024. That is unlikely, so PP is very probably right. One white offspring would have proved Pp.




Q7. Why is the F2 of a dihybrid cross 9 : 3 : 3 : 1? Answer in one line, using the monohybrid ratio.






Hint





Multiply (¾ + ¼) by (¾ + ¼).









Answer





Each gene on its own gives 3 : 1, and the two genes are independent, so the classes are ¾ · ¾ = 9/16, ¾ · ¼ = 3/16, ¼ · ¾ = 3/16 and ¼ · ¼ = 1/16. In short, 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 = (3 : 1) × (3 : 1). Mendel’s 315 : 108 : 101 : 32 collapses to 423 : 133 for shape and 416 : 140 for colour, both close to 3 : 1.




Q8. An Rr Yy plant makes four kinds of gamete, ¼ each. Explain this with what the chromosomes do in meiosis. When would it not be true?






Hint





Think of two homologue pairs at metaphase I. How many ways can they line up?









Answer





If R/r and Y/y are on different chromosomes, the two homologue pairs line up at metaphase I independently of each other. Half of the meioses put R and Y on the same side (giving RY and ry gametes); the other half put R with y (giving Ry and rY). Overall each of the four types is ¼. This fails when the genes are linked, that is, close together on the same chromosome. Then the parental combinations (RY, ry) are more common than ¼ each. That is the Linkage unit in Part 2.




Q9. In Aa Bb Cc × Aa Bb Cc, what fraction of the offspring is (a) aa bb cc, (b) dominant for all three traits, (c) Aa Bb Cc?






Hint





Answer each gene as its own monohybrid cross, then use the product rule.









Answer






¼ · ¼ · ¼ = 1/64. (b) ¾ · ¾ · ¾ = 27/64. (c) ½ · ½ · ½ = 1/8. A Punnett square would need 8 × 8 = 64 cells; the branch-line method or product rule needs three fractions.





Q10. A plant is heterozygous for 4 unlinked genes (Aa Bb Cc Dd). How many kinds of gamete does it make? If it is selfed, how many different genotypes can the offspring have?






Hint





Per gene: how many alleles can a gamete carry? How many genotypes can an offspring have?









Answer





Gametes: 2 choices per gene, so 24 = 16 kinds. Offspring genotypes: 3 per gene (AA, Aa, aa), so 34 = 81. With complete dominance there are 24 = 16 phenotypes, and the fully recessive class is (¼)4 = 1/256 of the offspring.




Q11. Two parents without cystic fibrosis (an autosomal recessive disease) have a child with cystic fibrosis. What are the parents’ genotypes, and what is the risk for their next child?






Hint





The child must have received a faulty allele from each parent. Which of Mendel’s crosses is this?









Answer





The child is aa, so each parent gave an a. Both parents are unaffected, so both are carriers: Aa × Aa. This is Mendel’s monohybrid F1 × F1 cross, and the risk for each child is ¼. The previous child does not change this: each child comes from a new, independent fertilisation.




Q12. “Dominant alleles are more common in the population than recessive ones.” True or false? Give an example from Mendel’s seven traits or from human disease.






Hint





What does “dominant” describe: a relation between two alleles in one individual, or a frequency in a population?









Answer





False. Dominance describes what the heterozygote looks like; it says nothing about how common an allele is. The Huntington disease allele is dominant but rare, while recessive alleles can be very common (in peas, all plants of a wrinkled line carry only r). Allele frequencies in populations are the topic of the Hardy–Weinberg unit.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
About this lecture
We cannot set up crosses in humans. To learn how a human trait is inherited, we read the family tree that already exists: the pedigree.

The standard symbols of a pedigree, and how to name each person (II-3).
The hallmarks of five modes of inheritance: autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked recessive, X-linked dominant and Y-linked. Mitochondrial inheritance gets a brief mention.
A strategy: do not try to prove a mode; rule modes out, one family at a time.
Risk calculations: the 2/3 carrier probability, partners from the population, and children of relatives.
Complications: incomplete penetrance, new mutations and ascertainment bias.

You already know Mendel’s laws, the χ² test and the probability rules (product rule, sum rule, conditional probability). Today we use all three. Book: Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter (pedigrees) and the chromosome theory chapter (sex-linked traits).

The whole lecture is one skill: look at a family tree and say which modes of inheritance it allows. Students already have the tools: segregation of one gene from the Mendel unit, and conditional probability from the probability unit. Today we only add two things: the drawing conventions, and the transmission rules for the X and Y chromosomes. Stress the strategy early: we rule modes out. A pedigree rarely proves a mode; it often excludes several. The risk part at the end reuses the 2/3 they met in the probability unit, now with a family attached.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Why humans need pedigrees
In peas or flies we choose the cross: true-breeding parents, a test cross, hundreds of offspring. In humans we can do none of this.

So we collect what already happened: who is affected, and how they are related, over as many generations as we can trace. One family is small, so a 3:1 ratio is rarely visible. Instead we look for patterns that are impossible under a given mode.

The point is the contrast with the Mendel unit. There we chose the parents and counted hundreds of offspring, so a chi-square test against 3:1 was natural. Here a family has two or three children, so ratios are useless within one family; with three children, 0, 1, 2 or 3 affected are all quite likely. What a pedigree does give us is structure: who passed what to whom. A single impossible transmission, such as an affected child of two unaffected parents under dominant inheritance, excludes a mode no matter how small the family is. That is why the analysis is about exclusion. Mention that clinical genetics still draws pedigrees routinely, now often next to DNA tests.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
The symbols


Generations are roman numerals from the top; people are numbered left to right within a generation, so “II-2” names one person.
The proband is the affected person through whom the family came to attention. Remember this: it matters for bias later.
Half-filled means a known (or obligate) heterozygous carrier. Most pedigrees do not show carriers, because nobody has tested them.


Go through the symbols quickly; they are a convention, not a concept. Squares are males, circles females, diamonds sex unknown. Filled means affected. A diagonal slash means deceased. A horizontal line between two people is a mating; a double line means the partners are related (consanguineous). The vertical line of descent drops to a horizontal sibship line, and the children hang from it in birth order, left to right. The arrow marks the proband. Some books mark X-linked carrier women with a dot in the centre instead of half-filling; we use half-filled for all carriers. Point out that carriers are only drawn when we know: either by a test, or because the logic of the pedigree forces it (an obligate carrier).

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Autosomal recessive


The affected person is aa; both parents are usually unaffected carriers (Aa × Aa), so ¼ of their children are expected to be affected.
The trait skips generations: it appears among siblings, often with no affected ancestor.
Consanguinity (a double line) is common: relatives are more likely to carry the same rare allele.
Examples: phenylketonuria (PKU), cystic fibrosis.


Read the figure from the bottom. IV-1 and IV-3 are affected but their parents are not: so the allele was hidden in both parents, which is the hallmark of a recessive trait. Both parents must be carriers, so III-2 and III-3 are obligate carriers even though nobody tested them. They are first cousins, which is the classic clue: a rare recessive allele from a shared grandparent can come down both sides. Both sexes are affected, as expected for an autosome. Note what is missing: no affected people in generations I to III. That is common for rare recessive diseases. Ask: what would rule out AR? Only two affected parents with an unaffected child, because aa × aa can only give aa.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Autosomal dominant


Every affected person has an affected parent (with full penetrance and no new mutation): the trait appears in every generation.
Affected (Aa) × unaffected (aa) gives ½ affected children, of either sex.
Male-to-male transmission (father → son) is possible. A son gets his father’s Y, not his X, so this rules out X-linkage.
Examples: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome.


The pattern is vertical: affected people in each generation, each with an affected parent. Most affected people are heterozygous, because the disease allele is rare, so the cross is Aa × aa and half the children are affected. Here 5 of 8: in small families, expect noise around one half. The key line is I-1 to II-2 to III-1: father to son to grandson. A father gives his son a Y chromosome, so a trait that goes from father to son cannot be on the X. This is the single most useful observation for separating autosomal dominant from X-linked dominant. What rules out AD? An affected child of two unaffected parents; we will see later that new mutations and incomplete penetrance can produce exactly this, which is why the assumptions matter.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Sex linkage, just enough for pedigrees
text:
Sex linkage, just enough for pedigrees
Recap only; Part 2 (Chromosome theory) covers sex chromosomes properly.

Females are XX; males are XY. A male has one X, so he is hemizygous for X-linked genes: a single recessive allele shows.
A father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son.
A mother gives one of her two X chromosomes to each child, ½ each.
Notation: XA and Xa for the two alleles on the X; XaY is an affected male for an X-linked recessive trait.

This slide gives just what pedigree reading needs; meiosis, sex determination and dosage compensation come in Part 2. The two transmission rules carry everything: fathers pass X to daughters and Y to sons; mothers pass either X with probability one half. From the rules, the two crosses in the table follow directly; have the students derive them with a Punnett square, using X^A and X^a as the gametes. The second row is the reason an affected man’s grandsons, through his daughters, can be affected: his daughters are obligate carriers. Mention hemizygous: males have no second copy to mask a recessive allele, which is why X-linked recessive diseases are much more common in males.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
X-linked recessive


Mostly males are affected; an affected female needs an affected father and a carrier mother.
Affected males are related through unaffected carrier females: the trait passes from grandfather to grandson via a daughter.
No male-to-male transmission: an affected father gives his Xa to every daughter and to no son.
Examples: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, haemophilia A, red–green colour blindness.


Point to I-2, a carrier woman: half her sons are affected (II-4), half her daughters are carriers (II-2). II-2 in turn has two affected sons among four children. This is the “knight’s move” pattern: grandfather or great-uncle to grandson, through women who are not affected. On the right, II-4 is an affected man: all his daughters are carriers (III-5), none of his sons is affected. What rules out XR? An affected woman with an unaffected son (she is XaXa, so every son gets Xa), or an affected daughter whose father is unaffected. Male-to-male transmission does not strictly rule out XR, if the mother happens to be a carrier, but it makes XR much less likely. The demo shows this case.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
X-linked dominant


An affected father has all daughters affected and no affected sons.
An affected (heterozygous) mother passes it to ½ of her sons and ½ of her daughters: here it looks just like autosomal dominant.
More affected females than males, often with milder symptoms in females.
Example: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX).


X-linked dominant is rare, and easy to confuse with autosomal dominant, because an affected mother gives the same one-half to both sexes under either mode. The families that decide it are those with an affected father. Under XD all his daughters are affected and none of his sons; under AD each child, of either sex, has a one-half chance. One unaffected daughter or one affected son of an affected father rules XD out. Females are more often affected because they have two X chromosomes, and therefore two chances to carry the allele. Females are often milder because of X inactivation, which comes in Part 6.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Y-linked and mitochondrial


Y-linked: only males, from father to every son. There are few Y genes; examples involve male fertility.
Mitochondrial: from the mother to all her children; fathers never transmit. Severity varies because cells carry a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondria (heteroplasmy). Example: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Full story in Part 5 (Organelle inheritance).


Both are quick. Y-linked inheritance is strict father-to-son, with no females ever affected, because the Y passes only from father to son. The Y carries few genes, mostly for male development and fertility, so Y-linked pedigrees are rare in the clinic. Mitochondria come from the egg, so the mother passes them to all her children and a father passes them to none. In real families the pattern is blurred by heteroplasmy, so not every child of an affected mother is equally affected; that is the topic of the organelle inheritance unit in Part 5. The demo and the exercises use only the four nuclear modes.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
A strategy: rule modes out
Do not ask “which mode is it?”. Ask “which modes are impossible?”, family by family. With full penetrance and no new mutations:







You see in one family

Check each mode against every parent–child trio.
Among the modes left, prefer the one that needs fewest extra assumptions, such as carriers marrying in from the population.


This is the slide to copy into notes. Each row is a single trio: father, mother, child. Each impossible trio is a proof that the mode is wrong, under our assumptions. Go through the rows and ask students to justify each from the transmission rules. For the first row under XD: an affected daughter needs an affected parent, and an affected son needs an affected mother, so both are ruled out. Step 2 is about likelihood, not logic: AR is almost never strictly ruled out, because any unaffected person could be a carrier. But if AR needs three unrelated people who married in to all be carriers of a rare allele, it is a poor explanation.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Consistent is not the same as proven
text:
Consistent is not the same as proven
A pedigree often fits several modes. Look at fig04 again (X-linked recessive):

AR also fits, if I-1 and I-2 are both carriers and II-1, who married in, is a carrier too. For a rare allele that is unlikely, but it is not impossible.
AD is ruled out: III-1 is affected but his parents II-1 and II-2 are not.
XD is ruled out: affected sons of an unaffected mother.

So we say “consistent with X-linked recessive”, and we prefer it because it needs no extra carriers. More families, or a DNA test, can settle it.


Students tend to want one right answer. Make the point that the honest result of pedigree analysis is a list of modes that remain, ranked by how plausible they are. In fig04, AR survives the logic test but needs the in-law II-1 to carry the same rare allele. XR needs nothing extra beyond a carrier grandmother. That is why we favour XR. In the demo, you can test each mode: it will report consistent or ruled out, show a set of genotypes that works, and name the people who married in and must be carriers.
