text:
Demo: which mode?




This pedigree was generated under a hidden mode. Test X-linked recessive first: it is ruled out, and the demo rings the trio, an affected mother with an unaffected son. Then test AD, XD and AR: all three are consistent. Ask the class which is most likely. Under XD the affected father I-1 must have all daughters affected and no sons; he has exactly that, and so does III-3. Under AD that pattern has probability one half per child, about 1/32 for these five children. Under AR, two people who married in must be carriers. Then press reveal. Press “new pedigree” for another family if time allows. The demo assumes full penetrance and no new mutations, so it can rule out a mode that a real family would still allow.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Risk 1: the 2/3 carrier probability
Two unaffected parents have a child with PKU (autosomal recessive). So both parents are Aa. What is the chance that their unaffected daughter is a carrier?

Aa \times Aa \;\rightarrow\; \tfrac14\,AA,\; \tfrac12\,Aa,\; \tfrac14\,aa

She is not aa, so we condition on “unaffected” (recap: Probability and the χ² test):

P(Aa \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{1/2}{1/4 + 1/2} = \frac{2}{3}.


The answer is 2/3, not 1/2: knowing she is unaffected removes the aa quarter.
Her parents are obligate carriers: probability 1.


This is the conditional probability from the probability unit, in a family setting. Students often say one half, because Aa is half of the Punnett square. But the Punnett square includes aa, and we already know she is not aa. Among the three unaffected quarters, two are Aa and one is AA. Draw the Punnett square, cross out aa, count what is left. Point out that the parents’ carrier status is not a probability at all: an affected child proves it.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Risk 2: a partner from the population
text:
Risk 2: a partner from the population
The unaffected sister (carrier probability 2/3) has a child with a man from the population. He has no family history. Assume a carrier frequency of 1/50.

P(\text{child } aa) = \underbrace{\tfrac23}_{\text{she is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac1{50}}_{\text{he is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac14}_{\text{both pass }a} = \tfrac{1}{300}.


Product rule: three independent events must all happen.
Where does 1/50 come from? If a disease affects 1 in 10 000 births, then q = 1/100 and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 1/50. That is Hardy–Weinberg, in Part 7 (Hardy–Weinberg).
If both partners have an affected sibling: 2/3 × 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/9.


Build the risk as a chain: she must be a carrier, he must be a carrier, and both must pass on a. Each is a probability and they multiply. The population carrier frequency is the weak link; it depends on the population, and for most diseases the clinic looks it up. Here we treat 1/50 as an assumption. Make clear that the 1/50 is derived, not looked up: incidence 1/10 000 means q squared = 1/10 000, so q = 1/100 and 2pq is about 2/100 = 1/50. The last line is a classic exam problem: two unaffected people who each have an affected sibling. Compare 1/300 with 1/9: family history moves the risk by a factor of about 30.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Consanguinity raises recessive risk
Relatives share alleles by descent from common ancestors. If one great-grandparent carried a rare allele, it can come down both sides of a cousin marriage and meet again in a child.

For a rare allele, an unrelated partner is almost never a carrier of the same allele. A cousin is much more likely to be, because the allele may be in the family.
The child of first cousins is homozygous by descent at about 1/16 of its genes.
This is why consanguinity in a pedigree is a hint for autosomal recessive inheritance, and why rare recessive diseases are more common in families and populations where cousin marriage is frequent.


Keep this qualitative. The one number is 1/16, the inbreeding coefficient of a child of first cousins: the probability that the two copies of a gene in that child are copies of the same ancestral allele. It does not mean the child has a 1/16 risk of disease: the risk depends on whether the shared ancestors carried a disease allele at all. The key idea is that relatedness makes the second carrier much more likely when the allele is rare. Do not moralise: in many parts of the world cousin marriage is common and most children are healthy; the increase in absolute risk is modest. Inbreeding returns in Part 7 with Hardy–Weinberg.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Complications
Our rules assumed full penetrance and no new mutations. Real families break both.

Incomplete penetrance (from Extensions to Mendel): a person carries a dominant allele but is unaffected. An AD trait then skips a generation and can look recessive.
New mutations: an affected child of two unaffected parents under AD. Most cases of achondroplasia arise this way.
Ascertainment bias: families reach the clinic because they have an affected child. Families with Aa × Aa parents but no affected child are never seen.

Each one can make a correct mode look “ruled out”, so read impossible trios with these in mind.

These three are why a real geneticist does not apply the rule-out table blindly. Incomplete penetrance: an obligate carrier, such as an unaffected parent between an affected grandparent and an affected grandchild, is the tell-tale sign. New mutations: for dominant diseases that reduce reproduction, many cases are new; an isolated affected child of unaffected parents is then expected, not paradoxical. Ascertainment is subtler and gets its own slide: it does not break transmission rules, it distorts ratios.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Ascertainment bias: the numbers
Take many Aa × Aa families with 3 children. Each child is affected with probability q = 1/4.

All families: 1/4 of the children are affected.
Families seen in the clinic (at least one affected child): the fraction is higher, because the families with 0 affected are missing. Expected affected per ascertained family:


\frac{n q}{1-(1-q)^n} = \frac{3 \times 0.25}{1 - 0.75^3} = \frac{0.75}{0.578} = 1.30,

so the fraction affected is 1.30/3 ≈ 0.43, not 0.25.
A naive count in clinic families would wrongly reject the 1/4 of a recessive trait. We simulate this in R in the exercise.

The denominator is the probability that a family has at least one affected child, one minus the probability that all three are unaffected. Dividing by it rescales the expected count to the families we actually see. With 3 children, 42% of Aa × Aa families have no affected child and are invisible, so the observed fraction is inflated to 0.43. With larger families the bias shrinks. Historically this was a real problem for testing Mendelian ratios in humans; corrections such as counting only the non-proband siblings exist. In the exercise students reproduce this with rbinom and replicate, then filter, and compare with this formula.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Summary

A pedigree is the human substitute for a controlled cross; families are small, so we look for impossible transmissions, not ratios.
AR: skips generations, both sexes, often consanguinity. AD: every generation, ½ of children, male-to-male possible.
XR: mostly males, through carrier mothers, no father-to-son. XD: affected father → all daughters, no sons.
Y-linked: father → every son. Mitochondrial: mother → all children (Part 5).
Rule modes out trio by trio; among those left, prefer the one with the fewest extra carriers. Consistent ≠ proven.
Risks: unaffected sibling of a patient 2/3 carrier; multiply independent steps; consanguinity raises recessive risk.
Watch for incomplete penetrance, new mutations and ascertainment bias.


Recap the two-step strategy once more, since it is what students will use in the exam: exclude by impossible trios, then rank what remains by plausibility. Remind them of the three numbers: one quarter for a carrier couple, two thirds for an unaffected sibling, one half for a dominant parent. Everything else is the product rule.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Where this leads

Part 2: Chromosome theory explains sex chromosomes and X-linkage in full, and LOD scores use pedigrees to map disease genes.
Part 5: Organelle inheritance treats mitochondrial inheritance and heteroplasmy.
Part 7: Hardy–Weinberg gives the population carrier frequencies we assumed today, and the inbreeding coefficient.
In the exercise: analyse pedigrees by hand, look up real diseases in OMIM, MedGen and ClinVar, and simulate ascertainment bias in R.


Pedigrees are not a dead end. In Part 2 the same family trees are used to find where a disease gene lies on a chromosome, by asking whether it is inherited together with a marker. The population numbers we assumed today come from Hardy–Weinberg. The exercise links today to the databases: OMIM and MedGen record the mode of inheritance of each disease, and ClinVar records which variants in a gene cause it.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test

text:
Background
Probability rules.

Product rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), if A and B are independent.
Sum rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), if A and B are mutually exclusive.
Conditional probability: P(B | C) = P(B and C) / P(C). In practice, cross out the outcomes that are ruled out, and count among the rest.
Complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Binomial. In n independent offspring, each with probability p of a given phenotype,
\[P(k \text{ of } n) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}.\]
\(\binom{n}{k}\) (“n choose k”) is the number of birth orders with exactly k affected children. For example \(\binom{4}{2} = \frac{4 \times 3}{2 \times 1} = 6\).
χ² goodness-of-fit test against a ratio given in advance:

State H0 as a ratio, for example 3:1, and turn it into proportions (¾, ¼).
Expected counts: E = N × proportion, where N is the total observed count. Do not round E.
\(\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E\) over all classes.
df = number of classes − 1.
Compare with the critical value, or compute the p-value = P(χ² ≥ observed | H0).
Conclude in words: “reject H0” (p < 0.05) or “fail to reject H0: the data are consistent with …”.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
By hand
B1. (product rule) In Drosophila, the cross AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd involves four unlinked genes. What is the probability of an offspring that is (a) aabbccdd; (b) dominant in phenotype for all four traits; (c) heterozygous at all four genes?
B2. (sum rule) From Aa × Aa, what is the probability that a child is homozygous (either AA or aa)? Which rule do you use, and why does it apply?
B3. (conditional probability) Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. Anna is unaffected, as are both her parents, but her brother has cystic fibrosis. (a) What is the probability that Anna is a carrier? (b) Anna’s partner has been tested and is a carrier. What is the probability that their first child has cystic fibrosis?
B4. (binomial) Two carriers of oculocutaneous albinism (autosomal recessive) plan five children. (a) What is the probability that exactly 2 of the 5 children have albinism? Write out \(\binom{5}{2}\) first. (b) What is the probability that at least one child has albinism?
B5. (binomial, sexes) Assume each child is a girl with probability ½. In a family of 4 children, what is the probability of exactly 3 girls and 1 boy? Is it more or less likely than exactly 2 girls and 2 boys?
B6. (χ², 3:1) Mendel’s F2 for cotyledon colour gave 6022 yellow and 2001 green seeds. Test H0: 3:1. Give E for each class, the χ² value, the df, and your conclusion.
B7. (χ², test cross) A Drosophila test cross vg⁺/vg × vg/vg gives 230 offspring with normal wings and 170 with vestigial wings. Test H0: 1:1. If you reject H0, suggest one biological reason.
B8. (χ², three classes) Flower colour in snapdragons (Antirrhinum majus) shows incomplete dominance. An F2 from red × white gives 52 red, 109 pink and 39 white plants. Test H0: 1:2:1. How many degrees of freedom does the test have?
B9. (which ratio?) An F2 from two white-flowered sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus) lines gives 382 purple and 269 white plants (illustrative numbers). Test the data against 3:1 and against 9:7. Which hypothesis do you reject, and which is consistent with the data? (The 9:7 ratio comes from two genes that are both needed for colour; see Extensions to Mendel.)

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Explore
Do the χ² problems by hand first. The demo starts with Mendel’s seed-shape data (5474 round : 1850 wrinkled) tested against 3:1. Filled bars are the observed counts, and dashed outlines are the expected counts. Change a count with − and +, or drag the top of a bar. The right panel shows the χ² curve for the current df, with the observed χ² marked and the tail (the p-value) shaded.



E1. Read off χ², df and p for Mendel’s data. Which class contributes more to χ², and why, when both classes deviate from E by the same 19 seeds?
E2. Press N: 100. The counts are set to exactly 75 : 25. Now drag the aa bar upwards (or press +) until p drops below 0.05. How many aa do you need? Then go back to 25 and lower the aa count until p < 0.05. Does the ratio “look” wrong to you at these points?
E3. With 3:1 and N = 100, press simulate under H0 ten times and write down p each time. How many of the ten are below 0.05? How many would you expect in the long run?
E4. Press simulate 1000×. Compare the grey histogram with the curve, and compare “% ≥ observed” with the p-value in the title. Then choose 9:3:3:1 and N: 20 and simulate 1000× again. What warning appears, and why does the histogram no longer follow the curve as well?
E5. Choose 1:1 and N: 20, then make the counts 12 : 8 (60% : 40%). Note p. Now choose N: 1000 and set 600 : 400 (drag the bars). Note p again. What does this tell you about using percentages in a χ² test?






Solutions: Explore





E1. χ² = 0.26, df = 1, p = 0.608, the same as on the lecture slide. The wrinkled class contributes 0.20 and the round class 0.07. The squared deviation is 361 in both, but it is divided by E: 361/1831 is larger than 361/5493. The same absolute deviation weighs more in a class where fewer seeds are expected.
E2. Note that N changes as you change a count, and E follows it. With 75 A_, p first drops below 0.05 at 37 aa (75 : 37, χ² = 3.86, p = 0.0495). Going down, it drops below 0.05 at 14 aa (75 : 14, p = 0.043). So with about 100 seeds, ratios from roughly 2:1 to 5:1 are all consistent with 3:1. Small samples cannot tell close ratios apart.
E3. Your ten values depend on how often you have clicked, but most will be well above 0.05; often none or one of the ten is below. In the long run 5% of honest samples give p < 0.05: that is exactly what the 5% level means. Each of those is a “false rejection” of a true H0.
E4. For 3:1 and N = 100, the histogram follows the df = 1 curve closely, and the fraction of simulations with χ² ≥ the observed one is close to the p-value. This fraction is a p-value estimated by brute force. For 9:3:3:1 with N = 20, the note under the buttons turns red: the aabb class expects only 20/16 = 1.25 (and the 3/16 classes 3.75), which is below 5. The simulated χ² values are then lumpy (only a few distinct values are possible) and do not follow the smooth df = 3 curve well, so the curve’s p-value is unreliable.
E5. 12 : 8 gives χ² = 0.80, p = 0.37 (fail to reject 1:1). 600 : 400 gives χ² = 40, p < 0.0001 (reject). The proportions are identical, but the evidence is not: χ² grows in proportion to N. Percentages throw N away, so χ² must always be computed from counts.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Find it
Mendel’s numbers fit his ratios remarkably well. In 1936 the statistician R. A. Fisher argued that they fit too well. Fisher’s paper appeared in Annals of Science, which is not indexed in PubMed, but the debate has continued in genetics journals that are. You will find some of these papers.
PubMed search syntax. Type into the search box at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/:

"Mendel's data": quotes search for the exact phrase, not the separate words.
Mendel AND Fisher: AND requires both words. (OR accepts either; NOT excludes a word.)
Mendel[ti]: the field tag [ti] searches only the title. Without a tag, PubMed searches all fields and maps your words to related terms.

Click a title to open the record. The abstract is under the title. The journal and year are in the line just above the title, and the PMID is listed below the abstract.
F1. Search for "Mendel's data"[ti]. You should get only a couple of hits. Open the one from the Journal of Heredity. Report its title, year, journal and PMID, and summarise its conclusion from the abstract in one or two sentences.
F2. Now search for Mendel's data without quotes and without [ti]. Look at the line “results” near the top of the page. Do you get more or fewer hits than in F1, and why? (Look at “Search details” under “Advanced”, or just compare the titles.)
F3. Search for Mendel[ti] AND Fisher[ti]. Find the paper by E. Novitski in Genetics (2004). Report its title. Then find a hit in the list that has nothing to do with peas, and explain why it matched your search.
F4. Search for "too good to be true" AND Mendel. Find the 2022 paper by G. Radick. Report its title and journal, and, from the abstract, when the “too good to be true” problem became widely discussed.






Solutions: Find it





F1. Click path: PubMed → type "Mendel's data"[ti] → Search. The two hits are Weeden 2016 and Hartl & Fairbanks 2007. The Journal of Heredity paper is:

“Are Mendel’s Data Reliable? The Perspective of a Pea Geneticist.” N. F. Weeden, J Hered 2016;107(7):635–646. PMID 27578843.
Conclusion (abstract): Mendel’s data do show a bias towards the predicted ratios. Real pea crosses do not naturally give ratios closer to expectation than chance (if anything the opposite), and omitting some experiments cannot explain the close fit either. The author could not decide between misclassification of ambiguous phenotypes and deliberate falsification, and suggests that Mendel’s paper is best read as a simplified, persuasive presentation of his model rather than an exact record of his methods.

The other hit is “Mud sticks: on the alleged falsification of Mendel’s data”, Hartl & Fairbanks, Genetics 2007 (PMID 17384156). It has no abstract in PubMed, but the full text is free in PubMed Central (PMC1840063).
F2. Without quotes and without the tag you get more hits. PubMed now searches all fields (title, abstract, keywords, MeSH terms) and maps “Mendel’s” to variants such as “mendel”, “mendels” and “mendelism”. The quotes and [ti] together ask for the exact phrase in the title only, which is much stricter. (The exact numbers grow as new papers appear, so we do not give them.)
F3. Novitski’s paper is “On Fisher’s criticism of Mendel’s results with the garden pea.” Genetics 2004;166(3):1133–1136, PMID 15082533. An off-topic hit is “Bioactivation, toxicokinetics and acute effects of chloroform in Fisher 344 and Osborne Mendel male rats” (J Appl Toxicol 2004, PMID 15211614). Fisher 344 and Osborne-Mendel are names of laboratory rat strains. Field tags match words, not meanings, so always read the titles of your hits. You may also see “Programs for Pedigree Analysis: MENDEL, FISHER, and dGENE” (1988), where MENDEL and FISHER are names of computer programs.
F4. “Mendel the fraud? A social history of truth in genetics.” G. Radick, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 2022;93:39–46, PMID 35313209. The abstract says the too-good-to-be-true problem was understood almost immediately after the 1900 rediscovery of Mendel’s work, but became widely discussed only from the 1960s, for reasons linked to Cold War geopolitics as much as to concerns about the objectivity of science.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
In R
R1–R3 check your hand calculations. R4–R6 introduce this unit’s new idiom: simulation under the null hypothesis with replicate(). replicate(n, expr) evaluates the expression expr n times and collects the results in a vector. If the expression contains random draws, every evaluation is a new random experiment. This lets you see the distribution of any statistic under H0, without a formula.

R1. chisq.test on Mendel’s data
chisq.test(x, p = ...) tests the counts in x against the proportions in p, which must sum to 1.
obs <- c(round = 5474, wrinkled = 1850)
chisq.test(obs, p = c(3, 1) / 4)

dihybrid <- c(round_yellow = 315, round_green = 108,
              wrinkled_yellow = 101, wrinkled_green = 32)
chisq.test(dihybrid, p = c(9, 3, 3, 1) / 16)
Check the χ² values and df against the lecture. Then use chisq.test to check your answers to B6–B9.


R2. χ² by hand, then the p-value with pchisq
pchisq(q, df) gives the area to the left of q under the χ² curve. The p-value is the area to the right, so use lower.tail = FALSE. qchisq goes the other way and gives critical values.
N    <- sum(obs)
expd <- N * c(3, 1) / 4
expd
chi2 <- sum((obs - expd)^2 / expd)
chi2
pchisq(chi2, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
qchisq(0.95, df = 1:4)
Confirm that chi2 and the p-value match chisq.test, and that qchisq reproduces the 5% row of the table in the Background.


R3. Family composition with dbinom and pbinom
dbinom(k, size, prob) is P(exactly k), and pbinom(k, size, prob) is P(at most k).
dbinom(2, size = 4, prob = 1/4)        # exactly 2 of 4 affected
dbinom(0:4, size = 4, prob = 1/4)      # the whole distribution
1 - dbinom(0, size = 4, prob = 1/4)    # at least one of 4
pbinom(1, size = 4, prob = 1/4)        # at most one of 4
Then answer: two carriers have 5 children. What is the probability that at least 2 are affected? Check B4 with dbinom as well.


R4. Simulate 10 000 F2 samples under 3:1
First write a small function that computes χ² from counts and proportions. Then write a function that simulates one F2 of 7324 seeds under H0 with sample() and returns its χ². Finally, replicate() it 10 000 times.
library(ggplot2)

chisq_stat <- function(obs, p) {
  expd <- sum(obs) * p
  sum((obs - expd)^2 / expd)
}
chisq_stat(c(5474, 1850), c(3, 1) / 4)

one_f2 <- function(N = 7324) {
  seeds <- sample(c("round", "wrinkled"), N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(3, 1) / 4)
  obs   <- table(factor(seeds, levels = c("round", "wrinkled")))
  chisq_stat(obs, c(3, 1) / 4)
}

set.seed(1866)
sims <- replicate(10000, one_f2())
length(sims)
summary(sims)
mean(sims >= 3.84)
The factor(..., levels = ...) makes sure that table() always reports both classes, even in the (unlikely) case that one is missing.
Now plot the simulated values as a histogram, on the density scale, with the χ² curve for df = 1 (dchisq) on top:
sim_df   <- data.frame(chi2 = sims)
curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(0.02, 8, by = 0.02))
curve_df$density <- dchisq(curve_df$x, df = 1)

ggplot(sim_df, aes(x = chi2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(x = x, y = density), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.263, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "chi-squared statistic", y = "density",
       title = "10 000 simulated F2 samples of 7324 seeds under 3:1")
Does the curve describe the simulations? What fraction of the simulated χ² values are ≥ 3.84, and why is that the number you would expect?


R5. How often is χ² at least as small as Mendel’s?
A p-value looks at the right tail: how often is the fit this bad or worse? Fisher’s question looks at the left tail: how often is the fit this good or better?
mean(sims <= 0.263)
pchisq(0.263, df = 1)
For seed shape alone, is Mendel’s fit suspiciously good?


R6. All seven of Mendel’s experiments together
The file data/mendel_monohybrid.csv has Mendel’s F2 counts for all seven traits (from Mendel’s 1866 paper, as tabulated in Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter). Compute χ² for each trait with your chisq_stat function, then add them up. The sum of independent χ² values is again χ², with df equal to the sum of the dfs (here 7 × 1 = 7).
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
mendel <- read_csv("data/mendel_monohybrid.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mendel <- mendel |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(n    = dominant + recessive,
         chi2 = chisq_stat(c(dominant, recessive), c(3, 1) / 4)) |>
  ungroup()
mendel |> select(trait, dominant, recessive, n, chi2)

total <- sum(mendel$chi2)
total
pchisq(total, df = 7)
Now check the left-tail probability by simulation. This time rmultinom() draws the counts for each experiment directly, which is faster than sample() for large N:
one_mendel <- function(sizes) {
  chis <- sapply(sizes, function(N) {
    obs <- rmultinom(1, size = N, prob = c(3, 1) / 4)
    chisq_stat(obs, c(3, 1) / 4)
  })
  sum(chis)
}
set.seed(1936)
sims7 <- replicate(10000, one_mendel(mendel$n))
mean(sims7 <= total)
Which trait fits worst, and which fits best? How often would seven honest experiments of these sizes fit as well as Mendel’s did? Relate your answer to Fisher’s argument and to what you read in F1.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. Take one gene at a time and multiply (the genes are unlinked, so independent). (a) P(aa)⁴ = (¼)⁴ = 1/256. (b) P(A_)⁴ = (¾)⁴ = 81/256 ≈ 0.32. (c) P(Aa)⁴ = (½)⁴ = 1/16.
B2. P(AA or aa) = ¼ + ¼ = ½. The sum rule applies because a child cannot be both AA and aa: the events are mutually exclusive.
B3. (a) Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa), because they are unaffected and have an affected child. Anna is unaffected, so aa is ruled out, and of the three remaining equally likely cells two are carriers: P = 2/3. (b) The child is affected only if Anna is a carrier and passes on a and her partner passes on a: 2/3 × ½ × ½ = 1/6 ≈ 0.17.
B4. p = ¼ per child. (a) \(\binom{5}{2} = \frac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} = 10\). P = 10 × (¼)² × (¾)³ = 10 × 1/16 × 27/64 = 270/1024 ≈ 0.264. (b) 1 − (¾)⁵ = 1 − 243/1024 = 781/1024 ≈ 0.763.
B5. P(3 girls, 1 boy) = \(\binom{4}{3}\) (½)⁴ = 4/16 = ¼. P(2 girls, 2 boys) = \(\binom{4}{2}\) (½)⁴ = 6/16 = ⅜, which is more likely, because there are more birth orders with 2 and 2.
B6. N = 8023. E(yellow) = 8023 × ¾ = 6017.25, E(green) = 8023 × ¼ = 2005.75. Both deviations are ±4.75 (22.5625 when squared). χ² = 22.5625/6017.25 + 22.5625/2005.75 = 0.0037 + 0.0112 = 0.015, df = 1. This is far below 3.84 (p = 0.90). Fail to reject: the data are consistent with 3:1. (A χ² this close to 0 is also part of Fisher’s point: see R6.)
B7. N = 400, E = 200 for each class. χ² = 30²/200 + 30²/200 = 4.5 + 4.5 = 9.0, df = 1. This is above 3.84 and also above 6.63 (p = 0.0027). Reject 1:1. There are too few vestigial flies. A likely reason is that vg/vg flies survive less well (reduced viability) than vg⁺/vg flies, so some died before they were counted.
B8. N = 200, E = 50 : 100 : 50. χ² = (52 − 50)²/50 + (109 − 100)²/100 + (39 − 50)²/50 = 0.08 + 0.81 + 2.42 = 3.31. df = 3 − 1 = 2, critical value 5.99. Fail to reject (p = 0.19): the data are consistent with 1:2:1.
B9. N = 651. Against 3:1: E = 488.25 and 162.75. χ² = 106.25²/488.25 + 106.25²/162.75 = 23.1 + 69.4 = 92.5, df = 1. Reject (p ≈ 10⁻²¹). Against 9:7: E = 651 × 9/16 = 366.19 and 651 × 7/16 = 284.81. χ² = 15.81²/366.19 + 15.81²/284.81 = 0.68 + 0.88 = 1.56, df = 1. Fail to reject (p = 0.21). The data are consistent with 9:7, which fits a model where two genes are both needed for purple colour.

Where this leads
The χ² test returns in almost every unit of Part 1 and Part 2. In Extensions to Mendel you use it to choose between modified ratios such as 9:7 and 12:3:1, in Linkage a test against 1:1:1:1 is the first sign that two genes are linked, and in Hardy–Weinberg you lose one more degree of freedom because the allele frequency is estimated from the data. Simulation with replicate() comes back in Drift and selection, where no formula is available at all.

title: Quiz: probability & the χ² test
text:
Short questions on the probability rules and the χ² goodness-of-fit test. Try each one on paper first, then open the answer. Unless stated otherwise, assume complete dominance and genes on different chromosomes.

Q1. Two parents are both Aa. A couple says: “We already have three unaffected children, so our fourth is bound to be affected.” What is the probability that the fourth child is affected (aa)?






Hint





Does one child’s genotype change the gametes that form the next child?









Answer





¼, exactly as for every other child. Each child comes from an independent egg and sperm, so earlier children have no effect. The 3:1 ratio is a probability for each child, not a quota for a family.




Q2. In AaBbCc × AaBbCc, what is the probability of an offspring with genotype AaBbcc?






Hint





Take one gene at a time. What is P(Aa) from Aa × Aa? Then use the product rule.









Answer





P(Aa) × P(Bb) × P(cc) = ½ × ½ × ¼ = 1/16. The three genes assort independently, so their probabilities multiply.




Q3. In the same cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc, what is the probability that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype for all three traits?






Hint





P(A_) for one gene is the sum of three Punnett cells.









Answer





P(A_) = ¼ + ½ = ¾ by the sum rule (AA or Aa). For all three genes: (¾)³ = 27/64 ≈ 0.42 by the product rule.




Q4. Two carriers of cystic fibrosis (Aa × Aa) have an unaffected daughter. What is the probability that she is a carrier? Why is the answer not ½?






Hint





Which cell of the Punnett square can you rule out, now that you know she is unaffected?









Answer





2/3. Knowing she is unaffected rules out aa. Three equally likely cells are left (AA, Aa, aA), and two of them are carriers. The ½ is the carrier probability before we knew her phenotype. As a formula: P(carrier | unaffected) = (½)/(¾) = 2/3.




Q5. Two Aa parents have 3 children. What is the probability that at least one child is affected?






Hint





What is the opposite of “at least one affected”?









Answer





1 − P(none affected) = 1 − (¾)³ = 1 − 27/64 = 37/64 ≈ 0.58. Adding ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = ¾ is wrong, because “child 1 affected” and “child 2 affected” can both happen, so these events are not mutually exclusive.




Q6. Same parents, 3 children. What is the probability that exactly one is affected?






Hint





How many birth orders have exactly one affected child? What is the probability of each order?









Answer





There are 3 orders (the affected child is first, second or third), so (3 choose 1) = 3. Each order has probability ¼ × ¾ × ¾ = 9/64. Total: 3 × 9/64 = 27/64 ≈ 0.42. In R: dbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 1/4).




Q7. A student tests 9:3:3:1 on four phenotype classes. How many degrees of freedom does the test have, and what is the 5% critical value?






Hint





For a goodness-of-fit test with a ratio given in advance, df = number of classes − 1.









Answer





df = 4 − 1 = 3, and the 5% critical value is 7.81. (For df = 1, 2 and 4 it is 3.84, 5.99 and 9.49.)




Q8. A test cross gives 62 Aa and 38 aa offspring. Test H0: 1:1 by hand. Do you reject H0 at the 5% level?






Hint





E = 50 in each class. Compute (O − E)²/E for each class and add.









Answer





χ² = (62 − 50)²/50 + (38 − 50)²/50 = 144/50 + 144/50 = 5.76, with df = 1. This is larger than 3.84, so p < 0.05 (exactly, p = 0.016) and we reject 1:1. The excess of Aa is larger than chance usually gives. One possible biological reason is that aa individuals survive less well.




Q9. A student reports “70% purple, 30% white” and computes χ² = (70 − 75)²/75 + (30 − 25)²/25 = 1.33 against 3:1. What is wrong with this?






Hint





What does χ² depend on besides the proportions?









Answer





χ² must be computed from counts, not percentages. Using percentages silently sets N = 100. With 1000 plants in the same proportions (700:300), χ² = 13.3, a clear rejection. With 10 plants (7:3), χ² = 0.13. The same proportions are stronger evidence when there is more data.




Q10. A χ² test gives p = 0.40. Which of these statements are correct? (a) The probability that H0 is true is 0.40. (b) If H0 were true, a χ² at least this large would occur in about 40% of experiments. (c) The data prove the hypothesised ratio. (d) We fail to reject H0.






Hint





A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true.









Answer





(b) and (d) are correct. (a) is the most common misreading: a p-value is a probability about the data given H0, not about H0 itself. (c) is wrong: “fail to reject” means the data are consistent with H0, and other ratios may fit as well.




Q11. In a cross with 12 offspring, a student tests 9:3:3:1 and R prints “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”. Why?






Hint





Compute the expected count of the rarest class.









Answer





The smallest expected count is 12 × 1/16 = 0.75, and even the 3/16 classes expect only 2.25. The χ² curve is a good approximation only when every expected count is about 5 or more. Collect more offspring, pool classes, or estimate the p-value by simulation (chisq.test(..., simulate.p.value = TRUE)).




Q12. Fisher found that over many of Mendel’s experiments, the total χ² was much smaller than its degrees of freedom. Why is a fit that is too good suspicious?






Hint





If H0 is true, what is the average value of χ²? How often should p be above 0.9?









Answer





If H0 is true and sampling is honest, χ² averages about df, and p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1: only about 10% of experiments should have p > 0.9. Mendel’s results sit near χ² = 0 again and again, which chance rarely produces. For his seven monohybrid experiments the total is 2.14 on 7 df, and P(χ² ≤ 2.14) ≈ 0.05. This suggests the data were filtered or classified with the expected ratio in mind, though not necessarily deliberately.
